speechtext:
Hon. P. E. BLONDIN (Minster of Inland Revenue) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 114, to amend the Adulteration Act. He said: This amendment pur-* .poses to enforce the law passed last year concerning the fabrication and sale of maple sugar and maple syrup by forcing the sellers of imitations to label such articles with a declaration making the pub-

lie aware that they are imitations. It also restricts the use of the word "maple" to the absolutely pure products from the sap, and it increases the minimum penalty for infraction of said Act from twenty-five dollars to fifty 'dollars.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

speechtext: My attention has been drawn to the fact that this Bill purposes to increase salaries, and that being so it is practically a money Bill that would have to be introduced by resolution. The resolution might be prepared and notice of it given to-day.

The outside service.

Is it the intention to have an adjournment at Easter?
I make this inquiry because, though I thought at one time that it would be possible to prorogue before Easter, or about Easter, it is evident now that we, cannot possibly have prorogation before Easter even if we were to sit every day, and we cannot do that, next Friday being Good Friday. Besides, we find to-day seven new Government measures brought before us for the first time. There are the three Bills of the Minister of Inland Revenue, an important resolution by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, and a still more important resolution by the Minister of Railways. That makes five. Then there are the two Bills from the Senate, which, as I understand, are Government measures, and which, while I suppose, not contentious, are still of great importance. This makes seven new measures to be taken up, added to what we have still unfinished. Besides, we have not yet the Supplementary Estimates for the coming year. So, it is absolutely impossible to contemplate a prorogation even within the coming week, and I ask, is it the intention to have an adjournment at Easter or not?

I do not abandon the possibility of reaching a conclusion of our labours this week. My right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) tabulates the new measures as seven. They are seven in number, but, so far as I know, the three Bills presented by the Minister of Inland Revenue, and the two from my own department, are practically non-contentious measures and very short; I think the House can deal with them very quickly. The two others that were mentioned may cause a little more discussion than these. We are practically very well along with the Estimates, and the Government measure which we have before us to-day I hope we shall be able to dispose of without too long a discussion. So that, with diligence and application, and the same good feeling that characterized the sittings of the House last week, I
think we can get the business very fairly well disposed of by Thursday night. However, as that may not be absolutely possible, though I hope that members on both sides of the House will work towards that end, I have given notice of a motion by which the House will be asked to adjourn -if it is to adjourn-from Thursday night until Saturday morning; and so we shall have Friday free, but no extended holidays at Easter. From what I have learned of the opinion on both sides of the House, while we are all anxious to do what is necessary and not to go away until that is done, at the same time we dp not wish to stay here an hour longer than is absolutely necessary. Many members on both sides of the House have expressed the wish that we should not have a long adjournment at Easter. I will move my resolution tomorrow; 1 hope that the right hon. gentleman will turn it over in his mind in the meantime, and that he will facilitate as much as possible the object we have in view.

There is no
desire on this side of the House-and our conduct has shown that-to prolong the session beyond what is absolutely necessary. I would not have risen as I have done were it not for the fact that these very important measures-that proposed by the Minister of Railways and Canals is of very great importance-have been brought before us at this moment, and such measures cannot be passed except with ample discussion. Then, I have to remind my hon. friend that the Supplementary Estimates for the coming year are not yet down. 1
As to the Supplementary Estimates, I think I can assure my right hon. friend that they will not be very numerous nor very extensive, and that they will be brought down to-day.

1.	Has a new regulation been made permitting American fishing vessels to sell and re-ship their fares in the ports of British Columbia?
2.	If so, what date did the regulation come into force?
3.	Does the regulation apply to vessels either wholly or partially driven by gasoline or steam?
4.	Does the regulation apply to the Eastern Coast of Canada?

1.	On the 8th November, 1897, an Order in Council was passed providing that-
Foreigners of foreign corporations bringing fresh fish in American bottoms to any port in British Columbia shall be permitted to land such fresh fish at such port, without payment of duties, and tranship the same in bond to any part of the United States of America, under such rules or regulations and conditions as the Minister of Customs may determine.
A further Order in Council was passed on the 29th day of January, 1898, viz.:

That until the Sth May, 1898, foreigners or foreign corporations bringing fresh fish in
[Mr. J. D. Reid.)
American bottoms to any port in British Columbia shall be permitted to purchase supplies at any port in the said province of British Columbia, under such rules or regulations and conditions as the Minister of Customs may determine.
The provisions of these Orders in Council have been renewed from time to time, and are in force now for 1915 as to ports in British Columbia, with additional provisions as follows:
Orders in Council dated March 9, 1915.
During the present calendar year (1915) foreigners or foreign corporations bringing fresh fish in vessels registered in the United States of America to any part in British Columbia shall be permitted to land fresh fish at such port without payment of duties and tranship the same in bond to any port in the United States, or to sell such fish in bond to such local dealer or dealers as may be properly and duly licensed therefor, under the regulations and conditions hereinafter mentioned, which dealer or dealers shall export to the same in compliance with the bonding requirements (without the right, however, in either instance to sell in Canada for consumption therein, or otherwise except in bond, any of such fresh fish so landed) ; and such foreigners and foreign corporations bringing fresh fish in vessels registered in the United States of America to any port in British Columbia, shall be permitted to purchase supplies, and ship crews for such vessels, at any port in the said province of British Columbia, the whole under such regulations and conditions as the Minister of' Customs may determine.
These Orders in Council are not based on the payment of any license fee by fishing vessels.
2.	Answered by No. 1.

It will be interesting to the House if I give a statement in a general way of the work that has been carried on by the Naval Department since the outbreak of war.
Preparations having previously been made to meet all contingencies which could be foreseen, it was only necessary to carry out or expand these preparations when war appeared imminent.
At that time the Rainbow had been commissioned for patrol duty in the Behring Sea and was therefore ready for immediate service, whilst the Niobe was laid up at Halifax with a care and maintenance crew on board, which ensured her being kept in such a condition as would enable her to be placed in commission at short notice. On the declaration of war the Niobe and the Rainbow and the officers and men serving in them, were placed at the disposal of the Admiralty. Arrangements were immediately made to commission the Niobe and to complete her crew to full sea-going requirements. This was done partly by the transfer of the Imperial officers and men of the sloops Algerine and Shearwater, which, owing to their small fighting value had been ordered by the Admiralty to pay off at Esquimalt, and partly by the inclusion of 100 Newfoundland Naval Reserve men; the remainder of the crew being recruited from men who had served in the British Navy and were resident in the Dominion. A large number of these volunteered their services and as many as necessary were

entered for service during the period of the war. As soon as she was ready the Niobe joined the squadron under the command of the Rear Admiral Commanding the North American -Station, in which she has been doing duty ever since. The Rainbow was despatched south from Esquimalt to guard the trade routes and protect the sloops Algerine and Shearwater which were proceeding north. These two vessels arrived safely at Esquimalt and since that time the Rainbow has been continuously employed in the protection of trade and other duties in the North Pacific, and on the coast of British Columbia, being under the orders of the Imperial senior naval officer on that station.
The Dominion Government on the out- . break of war purchased two submarines which were building at Seattle for the Chilean Government. The crews were recruited from officers and men in the Dominion, the Government being fortunate in this respect in obtaining the services of two retired officers of the Royal Navy who had had previous experience in submarines. These vessels also were placed at the disposal of the Admiralty.
Permission was also obtained from the Admiralty to use the Shearwater as a depot ship for the submarines. These tnree vessels have all been actively employed in the defence of the British Columbian coast.
Naval depots have been established at Halifax and Esquimalt, in the former place for the -accommodation of supernumerary ratings awaiting draft, and in the latter for the training of the Royal Naval Canadian Volunteer Reserve officers and men. A large number of other vessels, both Governmental and private, -are being utilized in connection with the naval defence of the coasts. They are being employed on the various services hereinafter specified.
The icebreaker, "Earl Grey," on her sale to the Russian Government, was transferred to this department to be sent to Archangel.
A crew of naval ratings was provided and the vessel was successfully navigated to her destination, the voyage of 3,000 miles being completed in 14 days. On arrival at Archangel she was turned over to the Russian authorities. The crew returned by ordinary -steamer.
As to the personnel; recruiting has been actively carried on to complete the "Niobe's" crew as previously stated and to obtain the requisite crews for the other vessels employed on subsidiary duties, prefer-'
ence being given to men with previous naval experience. The naval volunteers, which were established just previous to the outbreak of war, developed largely in the West, where some 400 officers and men are enrolled. These volunteers have done good service both ashore and afloat, a considerable number having served continuously in the "Rainbow" since the outbreak of hostilities, whilst others are in H.M.S. "Newcastle" and various vessels at Esquimalt, including the submarines and their parent ship the "Shearwater." Their training is being continuously carried on. The department has acted as recruiting agent for the Admiralty. A large number of Imperial service officers and men have been reached and arrangements made for their transportation from all parts of the Dominion to England.
As to harbour defence; all details connected with naval defence at defended ports are undertaken by this department. At certain ports in Canada: Halifax, Quebec and Esquimalt, an examination service was instituted before the outbreak of war and has been uninterruptedly continued. This is for the purpose of ensuring that no vessel with hostile intent shall enter the harbour and also to facilitate the ordinary flow of commercial ships. To this end every vessel entering the harbour is boarded outside the port and her papers, crew, etc., examined. If satisfactory she is allowed to proceed; otherwise, she is detained for further examination.
The mine sweeping was undertaken at the request of and after consultation with the Admiralty. At certain ports a mine-sweeping flotilla is provided. This consists of comparatively small vessels whose duty it is to keep the approaches to the harbour clear of enemy's mines. This entails daily operations on their part.
A number of vessels are employed on patrol duty on different parts of the coast, including the Gulf of St. Lawrence and Bay of Fundy. They are charged with the duty of keeping watch for hostile craft of all sorts.
In reference to wireless telegraphy and censorship it was found necessary at the beginning of the war to close a large number of stations. On the west coast the situation having now relaxed they have all been re-opened. In conformity with the procedure in other parts of the Empire, a censorship is imposed on all wireless telegraph messages emanating there-from.
All enemy merchant ships were ordered

to be detained on tbe outbreak of war, tbe arrangement for this being concluded with ' the Customs Department. The only German ship in Canadian harbours was the barque "Bellas" which was seized at Ri-mouski and has since been condemned in the prize court. The Austrian steamer "Ida" was seized also, but subsequently released under the days of grace allowed. Many important questions regarding contraband and neutral commerce are continually arising which indirectly affect the department and are dealt with accordingly.
As to coast defences; at certain places guns have been mounted and manned by naval volunteers; whilst in other places protection has been prepared by the provision of motor torpedo boats and mines prepared for laying in case of emergency. These operations also were carried out largely by naval volunteers.
A system for the collection and distribution of naval intelligence has been organized, acting in concert with the Imperial authorities.
In connection with the stores branch for H. M. C. ships and dockyards, the organization and systems undeT which the work of this branch at headquarters and at the dockyards is performed, had been maintained in full force as far as possible before the outbreak of war. While the ships were manned by reduced crews, it had not been considered either necessary or advisable to maintain in the dockyards the full stock of stores required when ships were in full commission. When affairs assumed a threatening aspect in the last week of July, steps were immediately taken to *supole-ment the stock of stores necessary to complete the ships for active service. H.M. C.S. Rainbow being already in commission and the state of affairs on the Pacific coast being critical, no efforts were spared to supply at the earliest possible date all stores required at Esquimalt. Large quantities of stores were transferred from Halifax dockyard and special purchases were made as necessary. All stores necessary for the commissioning of H.M.C.S. Niobe were obtained without delay. Clothing and equipment have been supplied for all entries of active service ratings and the Royal Naval Canadian Volunteer Reserve. Suitable arrangements were made for the messing of shore parties in various localities. H.M.C.S. Earl Grey was fully stored for her voyage to Archangel, and suitable supply arrangements made for the submarines and all fleet auxiliaries.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service

With the ships equipped
with the present boilers and machinery, Canadian coal is not considered suitable. The difficulty from the naval standpoint, as I understand, is that the use of Canadian coal shortens the life of the boilers. Also, it creates too much smoke. The use of the Nova Scotia coal with the present boilers and machinery would make so much smoke that the vessels could be detected by the enemy's vessels at a great distance away. That might be overcome, and I should think it could be overcome by using boilers of a different character. But, being British-built vessels, the Niobe and the Rainbow are equipped with the same sort of boilers as other British ships, and the use of Nova Scotia coal is not desirable.

All empty Admiralty colliers ' returning to Europe from this side of the Atlantic have been provided with cargoes. These included two shiploads of gifts from Canada to the Belgian relief funds. Arrangements have been made for the transportation to England of large quantities of stores purchased by the Imperial Government in this country and the United States.
The naval store officers at both dockyards have arranged on behalf of the Admiralty for the receipt, custody, and issue as required of large quantities of supplies of all kinds for the Imperial ships on the Atlantic and Pacific stations.
Regarding the naval dockyards at Halifax and Esquimalt, the work has since the outbreak of the war increased considerably, necessitating an increase in the personnel of these establishments and considerable overtime and nightwork. Halifax is being used as the base for vessels of the North Atlantic fleet, and the dockyard is being used for carrying out repairs to these vessels, including the Niobe, and also those necessary to the various auxiliary vessels which have been employed on the defence examination service, etc. At the Esquimalt yard the expenditure and personnel have increased correspondingly. Repairs have been effected to the Niobe, the submarines, the Newcastle, and other vessels, and, on the whole, the work has been efficiently carried out, having regard to the facilities available.

Soon after the outbreak of war, I felt, after consultation with my officials, that it was necessary to have some officer of higher rank than we had at that time at Esquimalt. We were fortunate in securing the services of a retired rear admiral of the British navy, Admiral Storey, who was living in Canada at that time. We sent him to Esquimalt, and since then matters have progressed very smoothly. The numbers employed in the different dockyards are as follows: in the Esquimalt dockyard there were 258 in August, 428 in September, 370 in October, 362 in November, and 289 in December, 1914. At the Halifax dockyard: in August, 419; September, 405; October, 396; November, 369 and December 378.
I now wish to make a statement with the regard to the radio-telegraphic branch of the Naval Department, and its connection with the war. Immediately on the outhread of hostilities, the following thirteen stations on the east coast were closed down, and the essential parts of the apparatus removed: Father point, Clark city, Pictou, Cape Bear, Cape Sable, Partridge island, (St. John), North Sydney, Sable island, Cape Ray, Point Riche, Harrington, Grosse Isle, Grindstone island.
These stations were closed down for two reasons. It was felt that it would be very unwise to leave them in such condition that if they fell into the hands of the enemy they could be used for their own purposes. In consequence, therefore, of a plan formulated by the Interdepartmental Committee before the war broke out, immediately on the outbreak of hostilities these stations were visited by different vessels and practically dismantled. As the wireless messages sent out by these different stations often interfere with each other, it was felt, too, that the operations of the stations that were left would be more efficient than they would be if the others were also in commission. The following eastern stations remained open for naval and commercial work:	Montreal, Three Rivers,
Quebec, Belle Isle, Point Amour, Fame point, Heath point Cape Race, Camper-down, and the transatlantic stations at Glace bay, Louisburg and Newcastle, a military guard being provided for their protection, and the necessary censor staff to censor all messages handled. On August 7, the small station apparatus from North Sydney was transferred to the transatlantic station at Glace bay, and the station at Cape Ray temporarily reopened to provide emergency communication 
between the transatlantic station and the outside world, in case of interruption of communication between the station and Sydney. The anticipated situation modified itself, and Cape Ray station was again closed down on September 12, 1914.
One of the alarming reports we received- it came from the Admiralty-was to the effect that hostile merchantmen were making arrangements to attack the wireless station at Glace bay. We got into immediate communication with Halifax. The next day, when we were in council, someone came in and said-this was reported in a special edition of the Ottawa Journal- that Glace bay was being shelled. During the early stages of the war this was the kind of rumour which frequently reached us, from sources which might be regarded as fairly authentic.
On another occasion we received information from a lighthouse-keeper way down the St. Lawrence river that a German man-of-war had passed through Cabot strait and was heading towards the river. We got into communication with points along the river, and notified the collector of customs at the port of Quebec. I have reason to believe, however, that the steamer seen by the lighthouse-keeper was not a German vessel, but one of the British vessels which were in the vicinity at that time. The lighthouse-keepers have all been furnished with diagrams or silhouettes of the war vessels, and this lighthouse-keeper thought that the vessel he saw was a German warship.
The eight stations on the Great Lakes were kept in commission, the officers in charge of the same acting as censors, a militia or police guard being provided in each case to protect the property.
The folio whig seven stations on the west coast were closed down at the outbreak of hostilities: Prince Rupert (Digby island). Dead Tree point, Ikeda Head, Point Grey (Vancouver), Triangle island, Alert bay, Estevan point. The following three stations were kept open for naval purposes: Gonzales hill (Victoria), Cape Lazo, Pachena point; each of them provided with a censor staff and a military guard. Telegraphic communication with the Queen Charlotte islands being entirely cut off on the closing of the Dead Tree Point station, and the naval situation becoming less acute, the Digby island (Prince Rupert) and Dead Tree Point stations were re-opened on September 22, 1914. On October 11, 1914, Alert bay, Estevan point and Triangle island were reopened; on October 13, Ikeda Head, and

on October 16 Point Grey; since which time all the stations on the coast have been in commission 'and, subject to censorship and naval regulations, are handling all the business possible.

I would take this opportunity of saying that the department feel and I feel very much indebted to Colonel Aemilius Jarvis, of Toronto, who rendered great assistance in connection with the enlisting in Toronto of naval reserve men who were subsequently sent to Halifax and placed on board the Niobe. His services were invaluable. He collected the men and gave his time to the work, and I take this opportunity of thanking him on behalf of the department for what he has done. I would also take the opportunity of saying that since the outbreak of war a great deal of extra work has been cast on the officials of the Naval Service Department; but from the deputy minister down, the civil and naval officers of the department have all discharged their duties in the most indefatigable manner, without complaint about the extra work. In the early part of the war many of them were engaged day and night, serving much longer hours than under ordinary circumstances, but without complaint and in a way that was satisfactory to me as head of the department and ought to be most satisfactory to the members of this House and people of Canada generally. I make this statement without drawing any distinction. All through the department the same loyal service has been given and there has been the same desire to do what could he done.
The House is aware that four young men who were graduates of the Naval College at Halifax and were serving as midshipmen on the Good Hope gave up their lives. Wfe .have now serving on the 'Berwick nine young men from the Naval College, and there are six more of the same class in other ships, and ten other Canadians are serving in Her Majesty's navy. I believe that if they come in contact with the foe they will do their duty in a way of which we shall be proud as Canadians and which will be in accord witTT the very best traditions of the British naval service.

The sooner we get to the country and get this Canadian navy idea knocked on the head for good and all, the better. For my part, I have been intensely disappointed to see the right hon. leader of the Opposition, and his lieutenants and supporters generally, egging on this Government to a great naval expenditure; and, strange to say, the Government does not seem to have fortitude enough to resist 
it. The other day we had an example of the positively triumphant manner in which the Minister of Marine was compelled to say that he would take the sum of $1,000,000 which he had formally and technically provided for certain purposes, and would actually make use of it and spend it. A navy and an Army are two different things. The army in this country has been a great success. It was suddenly called into existence, yet it is ready to fight, and when the war is over it will melt as suddenly away, or can be readily reduced to a peace footing; and the ordinary people of this country will have the satisfaction of being able to go about their business without having to appropriate continually a very large part of their earnings for the purpose of some absurd, bombastic expenditure on an army in the name of nationhood. But a navy is a different thing and must be established beforehand. It is a breakable sort of thing that may break up at any time, yet it must be fully and permanently established; and of course the members on the two coasts, of both parties, are only too pleased to see the people in the middle of this country-in the middle West and in Ontario and in Quebec -breaking their necks to pay taxes to establish fleets and naval units, or whatever you choose to call them, on the coasts. We can mine the approaches to this country- if we like; we can stop all ingress, and we can defend the country with our military; but what on earth do we want a navy for? A country with a population of 8,000,000, why does it propose to blow itself up like the frog in the fable and actually try to rival Great Britain and the United States and other great nations with a naval establishment, with something that must be put on a great practical basis, with all its training colleges and training ships and equipment, involving an immense expenditure?
And here we are told in an easy off-hand way, that for the future it will be necessary to appropriate so many millions more, and, as I have said, I am amazed and disappointed to find that the leader of the Opposition is the apostle of this new propaganda. The other day a very eminent Liberal in this House said to me, " Burnham, we will yet have the Canadian navy in spite of you fellows," and I believe they will. I believe they will have the Canadian navy in spite of the country, unless we go to the country pretty soon and give the people a chance to knock the whole thing on the head. It cer-

tainly should be made an issue before we commit ourselves to it. The people of this country regret that they have to make a great military expenditure. They regret that the necessities of the hour are such that they must comply with the demands for defence. But the people are paying willingly, and are satisfied that, apart from a few boots or bootlaces and things of that description they are getting their money's worth. There has been a great and energetic attempt to place Canada on a war footing, and it has succeeded in a way that very few could have thought possible. A few years ago we were an amateur nation. Now we have suddenly entered the great arena of waT and are able to take our part. That is one thing. But that a little nation like this should have two strings to her bow, have not only a great military establishment, but a great naval establishment as well, is in my opinion a betrayal of the honest toiler of this country; and I beg the Opposition to recant, to cease to egg on this Government to an expenditure which is absolutely unjustifiable in every way. The time may come when we shall have a hundred millions of people, and if they should want a navy and can afford to pay for it, all right. But surely we have enough to pay for now; surely the increase in taxation is enough to satisfy the most ardent supporter of taxation for purposes of expenditure. But no, it is not; they want more. And next year when we come back they will have thought out a great system of naval expenditure that will be highly satisfactory to.the maritime parts and exceedingly pleasant to our friends of the Liberal party, who will then be able to say:	"We told you so; we have now a
great Canadian navy; are you not proud of it?" But mark my words:	J am a very
humble individual, but I assure you that I know what the people in the middle of this country think. If they only had an opportunity of voting on the naval question, they would send this Canadian naval establishment higher than Gilderoy's kite. That is what they would do. I regard this thing as unwise and uncalled for in every way, and as something that in its way is unequalled. Of course, the minister has done his work well. We are accustomed to seeing him do his work thoroughly. But he has allowed himself to be shoved into this expenditure simply because there was no opposition to it. In this case we have not two parties met for the purposes of discussion, but a Government and an Opposition, both together apparently trying to
unite a great overwhelming tide in favour of a navy, which in my opinion is unnecessary and absolutely unjustifiable.

I cannot let
the occasion pass without offering thanks to my hon. friend for directing his criticism not against the Government, but against the Opposition. That is certainly flattering to us on this side of the House. According to my hon. friend we are carrying on the Government, we are imposing our views upon the Government, and the Government are submitting to our dictation. If we had an opportunity of going to the country I am afraid the Government would be knocked down for being so submissive to the Opposition.
I think so too.

We are a
people of some eight million souls. We have a country fronting on two oceans. Does my hon. friend believe that a country so situated can do without any naval service?
Perhaps not indefinitely.

It has to be
one thing or the other. You have to choose between a Canadian navy and contribution to the Imperial Government. At one time I thought the Government had taken their stand for imperial contribution. But no, they seem to have submitted to the Opposition, to have been egged on and bulldozed by the Opposition into a Canadian naval service. Well, I can stand it if the hon. gentlemen opposite can. The minister has given us a very interesting statement, very full, very complete, and I sincerely offer him my congratulations upon it. But he has spoken' to us only of the naval service. There is another service to which my hon. friend must give his attention, and that is the protection of the fisheries. My hon. friend has not told us what he is doing about that.

The Prime Minister has stated that the Government would welcome any discussion or inquiry as to the procedure to be adopted in the expenditure of this money. The vote in this Bill is a vote of credit and not an ordinary supply Bill. It is not a vote of credit given to any one department, and no department has or ought to have control of it. Consequently the method of expenditure in connection with this credit vote should be different from that followed in the case of ordinary supply voted by Parliament. We should have a statement from the Government showing the system under which they have expended the fifty millions voted m August last, and as to the system they propose adopting in connection with the expenditure of this credit vote of one hundred million dollars. It is true that in the printed document laid upon the table of the House there is a recommendation made by a committee, composed of the Auditor-General and some deputy ministers and officials of other departments, laying down a system of expenditure. For instance, a portion of this recommendation is as follows:
The principle of public tender should be adopted as far as practicable in the construction of works fir the purchase of materials and supplies, particularly when it reached or exceeded the amount of five thousand dollars.
It is quite apparent that this recommendation has not been followed in every instance. The House will, I think, be disposed to judge leniently of what occurred in the early days of the war, because it was not possible or easy for the Government to follow all the suggestions, but in the main it was a fair and businesslike suggestion, and should have been followed wherever possible. I submit that in connection with this expenditure of $100,000,000 which is to be voted as a credit to the Government, the principle of public tender should be adopted almost without exception. We are now past the stage when the Government might urge that they could be taken by surprise in connection with the

purchase of supplies for our troops, and it is now possible to exercise a great deal more care in future expenditure than was shown in the expenditure immediately after August last. I wish to ask if the Government requires any of these spending departments, such as the Militia Department and the Department of Trade and Commerce, to submit to the Governor in Council or to the Treasury Board an advance estimate of the probable expenditure which they are likely to make. This vote, as I have said, is not analogous to the money votes in an ordinary supply Bill passed by Parliament. The position of affairs under it has been well defined in a Treasury minute of the British Government of date 20th August, 1914 relating to a credit vote which was made in just the same terms as our own. That Treasury minute states a definition of a vote of credit:
The nature of a vote of credit is thus described in the Treasury minute of the 1st of February, 1880 :
"A vote of credit differs from ordinary army and navy votes, inasmuch as it is taken, not by the army and navy departments, but by the Treasury. The House of Commons, in fact, dispenses for the time with its power of control and grants a sum of money in gross and without the usual limitations to the Treasury as being the central department of finance, to which it leaves the responsibility of distributing the money in a manner best calculated to meet the emergency.
'In discharge of this grave responsibility, it appears to my Lords that they are called upon to require the department about to be entrusted with the actual expenditure of any part of the vote to submit to the Treasury- (which would be the Governor in Council in this case)-in the first instance a general scheme of the expenditure which such department proposes to incur."
This general scheme is meant, whenever practicable, to precede the vote of credit and to be presented to Parliament as a record of the grounds on which the vote is asked.; it stands, indeed, for the Estimates, more or less detailed for an ordinary vote on Supply. After the vote of credit has been granted it remains with the Treasury to deal with the issues from it; and my Lords are of opinion that such issues should be demanded by the spending department, in letters to the Treasury, explanatory of the proposed mode of spending them.
That is the substance of that portion of the Treasury minute of the 20th of August, 1914, or, speaking more correctly, it is a quotation from this Treasury minute containing the description of a vote of credit made by the Treasury Board away hack in 1880. I wish to inquire if it is the intention of the Government to require of any spending department a detailed statement to the Governor in Council of this
anticipated expenditure to he made by that department with all necessary information, before the Order in Council is passed authorizing the expenditure. In other words, according to the British parliamentary practice, this vote of money is given not to any department, but to the Governor in Council, and no one department is authorized to make any expenditure out of that amount before it has received the order of the Governor in'Council.
As I have already stated, this was done partially in the vote of credit of $50,000,000 made last year, but not wholly. As I have said, we will deal leniently with any departure from this policy in the early stages of the war, because the Government were probably in the same position as the British Government found itself in at the same period, unable to follow what was the well established procedure.
Now, another point, and one which also is referred to in the minute of the British Treasury of last August. They urge very strongly that no expenditures be mads out of this vote of credit which is not strictly referable to the war. In answer to a question placed on the Order Paper by the leader of the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laur-ier), we had the statement that "$50,000, being the contribution to the Belgian Belief Fund, had been paid out of the credit of $50,000,000 last year, and further that the payment for the million bags of flour sent as a gift to Great Britain was also made out of this vote. I do not propose provoking a discussion as to the propriety of making these two payments out of the war credit vote, but I wish to express my doubt, my very strong floubt, of the propriety of making these expenditures out of that vote. I think it is hardly businesslike, it is hardly what tne country anticipated, that our cash contribution to Belgium and the payment of our gift of flour should have been made out of this amount which we are borrowing at the moment directly from the British Treasury. I mention these cases to emphasize the fact that the Government should exercise great care in determining what expenditures should be made out of this war credit vote.
That is all I wish to say at the moment; but I think it would be well if we had from the Government a declaration as to the general policy and system to be adopted in respect of this expenditure-what control the Governor in Council intends to exercise over the expenditures made by the several departments, and what authority

they will require from each spending department. Also, I should like to Hear from the Government a declaration of Its policy as to the system of tender and contract as recommended by the committee appointed on the suggestion of the Minister of Finance. This, as I have stated, was not adhered to, and I should like to have from the Government a declaration that in this credit vote of $100,000,000 they propose to adhere rigidly to the system of tender and contract.

No one will quarrel with the proposition contained in the recommendation of the British Treasury read by my hon. friend the junior member for Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean). That is the constitutional method of proceeding, and that constitutional method of proceeding rules in our Parliament and in our executive departments as it does in Great Britain. I agree with my hon. friend also in his statement that this is not an ordinary vote; that these conditions are not ordinary conditions; that this vote of $100,000,000, like the vote of $50,000,000 already given, is the people's money in a very different way from money expended in the ordinary exercise of the executive functions of Government. It is the people's money in either case, but it is the purpose, and the strain of accomplishing the purpose, which to a certain extent gives a different earmark to these war credits from those borne by ordinary expenditures of Government. I quite agree with that proposition, and I think it is fair to say that if the very greatest caution, prudence and oversight should characterize the spending of moneys ordinarily appropriated by Parliament, if possible still greater care, prudence and foresight should characterize the appropriation and spending of this money. I do not suppose there is anybody on either side of the House who will find fault with that expression.
As to the manner in which this vote is to be expended. This is a vote, as my hon. friend says, for no particular department, and no department has any right to spend any portion of this money except by the authority of the Governor in Council. That is the general principle to be laid down, and that is the general principle that has been followed so far as circumstances would permit, and will be followed still more closely in the expenditure of $100,000,000 involved in this Bill. I do not think that members on the other side of the House 
who take a dispassionate view of it, and I am certain no business man who takes a fair view of it, as they generally do, would expect that under the circumstances which suddenly faced us in August of last year and for the three or four months imme-' diately following, that we could follow exactly the methods of expenditure ordinarily followed. We had to act on the spur of the moment, without previous preparation and in many cases without time or opportunity for consultation. So, the expenditure for the war during these three or four months was governed by peculiar conditions. As stated by the Prime Minister, and as shown by the documents laid before the House, these expenditures were made, and had to be made, without the more leisurely exercise of the authority of the Governor in Council. And it is quite possible that circumstances may develop from time to time which will make it necessary that certain expenditures shall be made outside of the general rule that is laid down. But these are less likely to occur in the future than in the past on account of the considerations to which I have referred.
As to this war vote, if any part of it is expended by the Minister of Justice, or the Minister of Naval Affairs, or any other department of the Government, it is only made after allocation of a certain sum of money to that department for certain purposes which are detailed more or less to the Governor in Council before the authority is given. I imagine that squares with the Order in Council and with the constitutional practice. For instance, if it is thought right that a certain part of this money is to be set aside for the purpose of internment, the Minister of Justice brings his report to Council, stating the circumstances and the requirements, and from time to time he gets a vote or an allotment by the authority of Council, which he expends. And when other money is needed along the same line, the Minister of Justice brings his report to Council. He informs Council what has been done, and if more money is needed an additional Order in Council is given, allocating money for the necessary expenditure. This is the practice that has been carried out in the latter part of the administration of the war vote, and this is the system which would be carried out in the allotment and administration of the war vote which the House is called upon to make to-day.
In the written document prepared by the Militia Department, which is over an affair of prices, it is stated there what was

done and why it had to be done. Council was faced with actions which had been done and which it was absolutely necessary should have been done. As the Prime Minister explained to the House, a full tabulated statement of these expenditures was made; they were sent by the Council to the Treasury Board, and the Treasury Board was asked to take these accounts and look into them. The Treasury Board was met with these conditions, that these were expenditures that had already been made, and made under the spur of circumstances. The main part of the duty of the Treasury Board was to examine into the vouchers, and generally into the regularity of the payments that had been made. This the Treasury Board did.
That applies to the expenditures which were made in the early months of the war. After that, as I have stated, reports were made to Council and the expenditures were authorized by Council. When the Minister of Militia comes to Council with his list of proposed expenditures, he acts, as does the minister of every department, on the report of his officers and special advisers detailed for that purpose. His requisitions for supply, I suppose, have been adopted in the Militia Council. Then they are brought to Council, they are considered by Council, and if, after such discussion as takes place, they approve themselves to Council, authorization is made for the expenditure.
With reference to the last observation of my hon. friend, as to tender and contract: I think the Prime Minister stated some little time ago that the principle of tender and contract was the principle that was to apply so far as it could possibly be applied. In respect of that there are difficulties which are apparent to any one who has had the administration of a departmental office under his charge. There are a great many cases that are of minor importance, each one of them involving no very great expenditure; and to submit these to tender and contract means to take a great deal of trouble often for very little advantage. Yet in such cases, I am informed, the department gets prices from people who make the article, and upon these prices an award is based. It may be that the prices differ to a certain extent. In that case, I am informed, what is considered a reasonable price, averaged on the prices received, is set as the price for the article. With reference to larger matters, prices are asked by the department, and as far as possible, the allotment is based upon a fair price ascertained by inquiries made of 105
manufacturers. It is the fact also that the policy of the department and the policy of the Government most certainly is that these tenders for articles shall be asked from, and contracts made with those who are the actual producers or suppliers of the goods. It can be put in this manner-that it is not the policy of the Government that these contracts shall be given to middlemen and brokers but that they shall go to the larger producers and suppliers of the goods. And I.think that, while you may find exceptions in the early part of the war, in the period of which we have spoken, many more exceptions than we would care to have, I think you will find also that under the later and more leisurely arrangement made by the departments and the Government, that principle is carried out. That is the principle which the Prime Minister has recommended decidedly to each of the departments, the Militia Department included, and that is the policy, which, I understand, the Militia Department is anxious to carry out.
I think I have answered all the questions of my hon. friend with the exception of one, and that is as to the class of expenditure properly referable t-o this war vote. My hon. friend has mentioned two-the Belgian contribution and the gift of flour by the Dominion Government.
Might I interrupt the minister to add another, the payment of $50,000 to the Intercolonial railway for carrying the goods of the relief committee.

In the memorandum which I have there are marked queries as to whether tnat is a legitimate payment to be made out of the war vote or not. This matter has been largely under the hand of the Prime Minister; I have just come into possession of some of these notes, in which I find that this query has been made. I dd not think it has yet been really decided whether that payment should be made from the war vote or not; the question is debatable. With reference to the others, opinions may differ. We must remember that although we are careful not to load up the war vote with ordinary expenditures, yet there is a fair region of debate within which it may be contended that certain expenditures are or are not properly referable to that vote. The Government does not make any allotment to the war. vote without a fair consideration of whether that allotment is or is not a proper charge upon it. t Take, for instance, the million bags of flour. What I want to keep in mind is that although one is a war



vote and the other is not, the $100,000,000 or the $50,000,000 is not a gift from the British people or the British financiers or the British Government; it is a loan, and we pay that loan and the interest upon it, just as we would pay the excess of expenditure over revenue during any one of these years by a loan which we would make on the British market. The two loans are similar in conditions; they must both be met by Canada, and the interest paid thereon. But with reference to these three votes: the Belgian relief; the gift of flour and the Canadian hospital in France, after due consideration it was thought that these expenditures might be fairly charged to the war vote. They involve in the aggregate a large sum of money. They are not ordinary expenditures, by any means; they are extraordinary expenditures. I am frank to say that the charging of these expenditures to the war vote was all the more readily decided upon when regard was had to the general state of the finances of Canada. This money had to be got somewhere; it had to be got out of loans in some form or other, and, as it was an extraordinary vote in each case, the conclusion was come to that it was fairly allottable to the war vote. I do not know that anything else was brought up by my hon. friend that I have not touched upon frankly and fully. I agree in tne sentiment that with reference to this vote most scrupulous care should be taken to see, in the first place, that it is efficiently administered, in the second place, that it is economically administered, and, in the third place, that it is honestly administered. For my own part-and I think I can speak for every member of the Government-I am jealous of one single ten cents of this war vote that goes to anything else than the objective for which this Parliament and the country authorized the appropriation; that is, to the prosecution of the war.

May I ask the hon. minister if he can give me the information which the Prime Minister on different occasions promised to bring down, namely: whether a committee of council was appointed to supervise war expenditures; whether that committee was appointed by Order in Council; what its duties were; whether it is still operative; whether that committee dealt with expenditures generally, or with the expenditures of any particular department: if so, of what department?

The Dominion
Government, through its different departments, has been executing orders from foreign governments for war materials: saddlery, blankets, harness, hay, oats, etc. A sub-committeo of council was elected to allot the orders which were sent to us by the British, Russian or French Governments in respect of .war material that they required, and which they asked us to obtain for them at certain rates and under certain conditions. Whilst the purchase of those different supplies was entrusted to different departments, this sub-committee was appointed to make the allotments. That committee was also empowered to advise the Minister of Militia in respect of certain allotments or possible contracts required for Canadian troops. It has been in existence since September or October, I think; it has had charge of the former class of contracts in the way of allotment, and has consulted on several occasions with the Minister of Militia as to contracts for distinctively Canadian supplies required for the purpose of prosecuting the war, and paid for out of this war vote.
Mr. MACDONAi,D: Who were the members of that committee?

The personnel
of the committee has been somewhat changeable. It consists of some six or eight members ol the Cabinet.

Was it appointed
under Order in Council?
No, it was appointed by and acts under the authority of the Prime Minister.
Who were the first members of that committee?

From memory, the Minister of Public Works, the Minister of Trade and Commerce, the Postmaster General, the Minister of Justice, the Minister of Customs; later there were joined to it the Minister of Railways, the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Marine and Fisheries. That is, as I remember, the committee.
Was there a chairman of the committee, and, if so, which of the members was chairman?

The chairman of the committee was the Minister of Public
Works.
From the first?

From the first;
and I have been doing, without fee or reward, most of the clerical work.
Was the Minister oi Militia on that committee?

When the committee was formed, the Minister of Naval Affairs was acting Minister of Militia, and he w'as placed on that sub-committee because he was administering the Department of Militia; so that the Minister of Militia is also a member of that committee for the purpose of allotting Canadian supplies.
Was he not chairman foi a while-the acting minister?

No, the Minister of Marine and Fisheries was never the chairman of the sub-committee; that had one chairman only. But when that subcommittee sat with the Minister of Militia to advise as to contracts, the Minister of Militia during that session and in his own department was, of course, the chairman of that committee. You will make the distinction between those two duties:	the subcommittee was separated entirely from the Minister of Militia or the Department of Militia, when they were making contracts for the allied governments; but when they were advising with the Minister of Militia as to contracts in his immediate department the committee met with the Minister of Militia or the acting Minister of Militia and he was the one who presided.

I think it is well that
these observations have been made by the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean) and also those in reply by the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster). It makes very clear what, of course, the members understood before, that in a vote of this kind the Government as a whole is more directly responsible than it is in a regular departmental vote, although government responsibility is understood, no matter what the vote may be, departmental or otherwise. In a vote of this kind the Government as a whole is more distinctly and thoroughly responsible for every dollar that is spent. The manufacturers of Canada, for whom I have no brief, have been called on to do a good deal of prompt and extraordinary work. In the main I think they have responded to that call very well. I know a good many of them who have expended large sums of money in purchasing plant in order that 1054
they may meet the demands of this Government, as well as the demands of the Allies, in furnishing munitions of war. However, there have been cast certain reflections which may, if not cleared up, be discreditable to the manufacturers. The reason I mention this is that this is really the testing time for the industries of Canada. They have it in their hands to make for themselves a great name or to injure our future as an industrial community. A good many questions have been asked, some imputations have been cast, and there have been statements as to the necessity the manufacturers found of dealing through a third person instead of being able to deal directly with the Government. We have had it in evidence that certain manufacturing establishments were compelled to deal indirectly instead of directly with the Government.' The manufacturers of Canada have an association which is their official organization: all the leading manufacturers', and I imagine most of the smaller manufacturers as well, are connected with that association, which in very active and very strong and very influential. I cannot conceive that this great association would allow its members to be thus compelled to deal indirectly with the Government without making some protest, If they did I would mistake the calibre of the men very much, and would not have much sympathy for them. Have the Manufacturers' Association as an association officially protested through any of their officers to the Prime Minister the acting Prime Minister, or any member of the Government, as to the methods of purchase employed by the Government, more particularly as to the statement made that they were compelled in many cases to deal through a third party and could not sell directly to the Government? If there have been any such protests from the Manufacturers' Association, would the Government lay that correspondence on. the table before the clbse of the session so that manufacturers may have their side of the case before the public as well as the Government and Parliament? I think that would be but fair, if there be such correspondence.

I join with my
hon. friend in his sentiment that the manufacturers and producers in Canada have evinced a disposition to rise to the occasion and to represent Canada at its best in the call that was made for supplies in this country. I may explain that they have been anxious to do that and have aided in

doing that and have co-operated in doing that very thing. As regards the other point, of middlemen or direct negotiation, I may say, if my hon. friends will allow me to refer to my department, that the practice is to shut down absolutely on the middleman in respect of whatever contracts my department may have to make for outside governments. In the case of the French blanket order, which is a good illustration, the French Government asked this Government to supply, or to have supplied, 400,000 blankets of certain dimensions and of certain quality. We took that up and it was left to my department to see what could be done. I immediately got in communication with every mill that could make blankets in the Dominion of Canada and asked them directly from the department, how many blankets of that quality they were prepared to manufacture within the time specified. A great many people came to me asking for specifications. My first question to every one was, "What mill do you represent"? And if he did not represent a mill, he had no further converse with me about that. What I proposed to do, and what was done, was to make the contracts absolutely direct with the mills themselves. That was carried out, and I think that is in principle what every other member of the Government carried out, or desired to carry out. Now, I will say this. Though it did not happen in my department that the middleman was at all a profitable or necessary man to come in between myself and the mills, I think there are occasions and there are certain articles where you would, perhaps, have to negotiate through the middleman. Every member of the Government has to exercise a certain amount of common sense with reference to that. I will not carry that any further, but I just make it as a suggestion which I think will appeal to business men. I do not believe that instances of that are very many, but I believe it does occur in certain lines of enterprise and manufacture that you will have to deal with the broker or the agent rather than with the original himself. I think that answers the first part of the question of my hon. friend. I may say that at a very early period in these operations of supply and demand last autumn, the Prime Minister himself issued a letter of instructions to the members of his Government along that very same line, namely, that, as far as it could possibly be done, the original supplier or dealer should be the one who was negotiated with. In that letter I think 
he also expressed the wish that if any minister felt that a different course ought to be pursued in any case, he would consult with the Prime Minister before going outside of those instructions. Now, as to what the manufacturers thought or did not think with reference to its being possible for them to approach the Government except through a middleman, I do not remember any direct communications of that sort from them. I have had a great deal of communication with the Manufacturers' Association. Whenever I received an inquiry as to sources of supply and amount of output with reference to something I did not know very much about, my practice has been to communicate with the secretary of the Manufacturers' Association, and get from him the names of all parties who might be applied to in respect to that particular line of goods. I think that answers my hon. friend as nearly as I can answer him.

It is very interesting, but I am afraid it does not answer my question. What I asked was this: Did the Prime Minister, or in his absence the acting Prime Minister or any member of the Government, have correspondence with the Manufacturers' Association as a body, or with any of its officers, in regard to the manner in which contracts were being let, with particular reference to the fact that manufacturers throughout Canada were in many instances compelled to do their business through a third party instead of doing it direct with the Government. What I asked was, if there was such correspondence, would my hon. friend lay it on the table of the House before the session closed?

I have no recollection of such correspondence. If such correspondence took place, it would very likely be with the Prime Minister, and I have no knowledge of the Prime Minister's having received anything of that kind. The Prime Minister is absent now from a cause which of course we all deplore, but he will be back in the House before the session ends and will be able to answer.for himself in regard to that correspondence.
I do not wish to unduly delay the committee, but my question refers to any member of the Government, as well as to the Prime Minister and the acting Prime Minister.
I have spoken for myself.

My hon. friend has spoken for himself, and to-day he is the Government so far as this question is concerned. If there be such correspondence, would my hon. friend make a note and see that it is brought down?

I will make a note of it, but I will not say that the correspondence will be brought down. I will bring the matter to the attention of the Prime Minister on his return, and if there is anything that can be brought down I have no doubt he will bring it down. But my hon. friend, as a member of the preceding Government, knows that he has received many and many a letter sent to him confidentially which he could not bring down.
I understand that, but I had reference to official correspondence with the Manufacturer's Association as a body.
Then my hon. friend has his reply. I will bring the matter to the Prime Minister's attention on his return.

As I happen to be a member of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, possibly I may be able to answer to a certain extent the hon. gentleman's question. As far as I am concerned, or as far as any company in which I am interested is concerned, the Manufacturers' Association has nothing whatever to do with them as far as their sales are concerned, unless it might be that we were asking for information about exports. But as far as sales within the Dominion of Canada are concerned, even to the Government, the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, as far as my knowledge goes, has nothing whatever to do with them. There has been a great deal of talk about the third person. I should like to know what constitutes the third person. For instance, in my business and other businesses with which I am connected, there are what are called commission agents. These agents undertake to sell the output of the mills. Now, there must be a certain loyalty between the manufacturers and their commission agents to this extent, Sometimes we get orders direct from the wholesale trade; that is, the order comes direct to the mill, and not through our agents. In such a case, instead of sending the invoice direct to the merchant who gave us the order, we send it to our agent just as if he had taken the order himself; and he gets his commission on that order.
That commission being paid by yourself.

Yes. Even if we were to get an order direct from the Government *-we have not had that good fortune so far- we should send the invoice to our commission agent, not to the Government. The Government would get the goods just as cheaply through the commission agent as they would from us direct. The mill in all cases pays the commission. So there is not so much force as some might think in this talk about the third person. If the third person bought goods from the manufacturer and then sold them at a profit that would - alter the case. But there is a vast difference between the third person in that case and the third person who acts as a commission agent for a mill.
And who has a permanent engagement.

That is the regular business machinery of a large institution. I understand that thoroughly, but it>
was not that I was referring to. If I were buying a large amount of goods from my hon. friend, I should receive them in just the same way.

My hon. friend the Alin-ister of Trade and Commerce states that in making purchases for the allied Governments, they felt, and very properly, that a certain responsibility was cast upon them, and that in cases where he was concerned he sent notices direct to the manufacturers.
It was stated here by the hon. Alinister of Militia and Defence (Major General Hughes) that a contract was negotiated in the United States for ammunition for the British Government, I think, amounting to
75,000,000 rounds, that the .contract was negotiated by Mr. J. Wesley Allison, but. that subsequently the minister and a representative of the manufacturers met somewhere in the Adirondack mountains and * executed the formal contract. I would like to ask if that matter came to the notice of the Alinister of Trade and Commerce and of the Government as a whole.

Before my
hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce replies, I desire once more to correct my hon. friend the member for St. John. He has mis-stated the case absolutely, * and he knows that he has not stated it correctly. Air. J. Wesley Allison did not primarily negotiate the contract. 1 negoti-

ated it first with some of the hon. gentleman's friends in New York and in Cincinnati. One of the firms whose representatives I met asked $42.50 per thousand and the other Flint & Company, whom my hon. friend knows, asked $37.50. Then Mr. Allison stepped in and reduced the price to $33 for Mark vii ammunition, only $3 more than the British Government some weeks before, but during the war, had paid that same firm for Mark vi ammunition, which is about $5 cheaper than Mark vii. Thirty dollars per thousand rounds was what the British Government were paying for Mark vi and $33 was the price paid for Mark vii.

I do not think my hon. friend The Minister of Militia and Defence has contradicted the statement I have made, that Mr. Allison negotiated for the purchase of 75,000,000 rounds of ammunition which resulted in a formal contract being signed by the minister on behalf of the British Government somewhere in the Adirondack mountains-I forget the name of the place. That the negotiations were carried on by Mr. Allison I think the minister himself admits.
No, the negotiations were carried on by the Minister of Militia.

What the minister
said was that at the beginning of the negotiations he found that the prices were higher than he thought they ought to have been, and then Mr. Allison stepped in and got the prices reduced. If that does not mean that Mr. Allison carried on the negotiations to a conclusion then I do not know what language means. I think I would be entirely correct, in view of the minister's statement and in view of what he stated here a short time ago, in saying that Mr. Allison did carry on the negotiations. Now, I would like to ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce if the Government took any steps to get information as to the negotiations which were carried on by Mr. Allison in the United States with the different leading manufacturers of ammunition and which negotiations were carried on under credentials from this Government on behalf of the British Government and other of the allies?

My hon. friend asks me whether the Government took any steps to inquire into the negotiations which have been undertaken by Mr. J. Wesley Allison for military or war supplies in the United States.
[Mr. Sam. Hughes.!
For the British Government under credentials of this Government.

As far as I am concerned, I do not know of any steps that were taken by the Government in that respect. The question of supplies, and as to how they were provided, ran itself into two classes. All supplies, other than munitions of war, the Prime Minister-I am speaking with reference to orders from allied governments-directed the ministers of the different departments to purcha."' as it was thought best, some taking one thing and some taking another. In regard to munitions of war, it was directed that these should be negotiated for and provided for under the control of the Minister of Militia, and with those I have had no particular concern other than the concern which comes to every member of the Government when reports are made to Council submitting certain acts for approval, when I used my own judgment, as other members of the Government do, in approving or not the proposals that are made.

Let me say to my hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce that there are current rumours which seem to be well founded. I am not able to say whether they are absolutely well founded or not; but I think they are de-
4 p.m. serving of the attention of the Government, because if there is no truth in these rumours it -ii desirable that they should be set at rest, particularly as they concern purchases which have been made by the Allies under circumstances which necessarily have resulted from action by this Government. I am informed that this Government did employ the agency of secret service officers who were sent to New York, and who ascertained that the British Government could have obtained this ammunition at the prica of $25 per thousand rounds but for the intervention of Mr. J. Wesley Allison in New York, under credentials from this Government or one of the ministers of this Government. I am informed that the price of this ammunition was raised from $25 per thousand rounds, which was the figure first named and at which the British Government could have purchased it, to $26.50, and to that extent the manufacturers benefited. I am informed that the price actually charged the British Government was $33 per thousand rounds, which left a difference of $6.50 per thousand as Mr. Allison's profit. On 75,000,000 rounds my hon. friend will see that that will amount

to somewhere between $400,000 and $500,000 on that one order. It is rumoured-my hon. friend can ascertain whether it is true or, not-that the Government, or some members of the Government-perhaps the Prime Minister-sent members of the secret service to New York city, and that the result of the investigation of the two gentlemen who were sent there has been to verify the statement which I have made. I do not vouch for it; if it is not correct it ought to be made known that it is not correct. It does not reflect up">n the Government unless the Government was a party to it or countenanced it, aui of course the Minister of Trade and Commerce will agree with me that the Government should not countenance it. It is stated also that as a result of these introductions which be had, and on these conditions which he was able to make, Mr. Allison was able to control the' ammunition supply coining from these large manufacturers, and he formed a company called the Allison Supply Company. I find in the Montreal Star of the 26th of March this statement, showing the magnitude of the operations which Mr. Allison is carrying on:
The Allison Supply Company of Canada announced that they had let contracts with United States manufacturers for 535,000,000 rounds of ammunition for the European Allies. The company has contracts pending for 500,000,000 additional rounds of ammunition. J. Wesley Allison, of Morrishurg, is stated to be the head of the company.
This statement in the Montreal Star is in accord with statements made to rue by gentlemen in New York who profess to know. I regard it as a very serious matter. We find that instead of the allied governments being able to do what the Minister of Trade and Commerce-I judge from his remarks in reference to buying blankets for the French Government-says they ought to be able to do, namely, to buy on the most favourable possible terms directly from the manufacturers, they are buying through the Allison Supply Company, which has* obtained credentials from this Government. We find this company formed by Mr. Allison; we find it continuing its work, occupying the position of middlemen and supplying this large quantity of ammunition to the Allies. It may be said that this is the business of the allied governments, and I admit that would be a natural answer to make, if it is not a fact that through his credentials received from-this Government, Mr. Allison or his company has been asked, by the British Government, to purchase
ammunition, and has been enabled to effect a combination with the manufacturers which gives him the control of the busine-s of furnishing ammunition, and as a result has been able to get himself, or the company he has formed, into the position of middlemen, through whom the allied governments are obliged to make their contracts, instead of making them directly with the manufacturers. I am informed that the Government has information on the matter already, but if it has not it ought to get that information and supply the information to the House.

The hon. gentleman has spoken of rumours, hut he has not honoured the House by giving any. He has not taken the usual course that even an ordinary back-bencher would take, of furnishing the House with the slightest bit of data on the subject. I will tell him something. Early in the war, the Militia Department, having successfully negotiated to save the British Government $9.50 per thousands rounds of ammunition, was requested to obtain a contract from the United States authorities for the manufacture of 200,000 shells, prices were obtained, deliveries were asked for, and it was found that the prices were abnormally high compared with what we could make them in Canada for, and the deliveries were very slow. I am anxious to educate the hon. gentleman from St. John, and I trust he is listening to me.

I am listening most
attentively.

The matter
dragged on for a time, when I conceived the notion of calling the manufacturers together. I knew that our foundries, owing to the war, were not carrying on their usual business. I knew that our large steam plants were more or less reducing output, and I called a meeting of the large manufacturers of iron and steel of the Dominion of Canada together-I do not want my hon. friend (Mr. Pugsley) to lose a word of this.
What has this got to do with the question of small-arms ammunition to which I have referred?

I know that
my hon. friend is sometimes so dense and thick-headed that it takes an awful lot of pounding to get it in, but it is going in, or I will know the reason why. The manufacturers were called together and the lacls were placed before them, and they were asked to appoint a committee to go to the

arsenal at Quebec and witness the manufacture of ammunition. They went there, and after spending several days, they came to the conclusion that we could make ammunition in Canada. Accordingly, a committee was formed of the most representative men that could be found-I will not say the most representative men that could be found, but I will say they were all representative men. I appointed a shell committee and entrusted them with the management of that work, and I think I am safe in saying that everything except the driving bands of copper and the fuse is today made in Canada, and that applies not only to the ordinary 18-pound and 15-pound shells, but to the larger shells as well. At present$57,000,000 has been contracted for throughout the length and breadth of the Dominion of Canada, and more than that large sum is forthcoming to the shell industry. I understand that Mr. Allison on his own responsibility-he is a free citizen, he does not owe any allegiance, thank Heaven,. to either the Minister of Militia and Defence for Canada or to the hon. member for St. John-Mr. Allison, profiting by the experience of Canada in this regard, and knowing that the Russian Government was very short of shells, made a contract with that Government for 5,000,000 shells- that is what the hon. member refers to-
5,000,000 shells and not 500,000,000, which are being manufactured to-day.

Will my hon. friend
pardon me? This article in the Montreal Star does not refer to shells; it refers to rounds of ammunition. The hon. gentleman is speaking of a different matter entirely.

Is that so? I can tell the hon. gentleman there is nothing to it. These 5,000,000 shells were manufactured by a company of which a Canadian corporation is at the head, and they are being manufactured in Canada and the United States, and many millions of dollars will be left in Canada, and many millions also will be left in the United States. Let me say that a new company, owned in Canada, will he interested in this matter, and it is a new industry entirely brought to this country.

The statement of the Minister of Militia is very interesting, but he has been dealing with a different matter entirely from that to which I was referring. He is referring to a contract which Mr. 
Allison, I am informed, succeeded in getting for the manufacture of shells for the Russian Government; a contract in which the Hon. Senator Curry is interested, as I have seen stated in the newspapers. That refers to a contract for shells to be manufactured as far as possible in Canada, and I hope they will be manufactured in Canada. But what I am speaking of is an entirely different matter; I am referring to ordinary ammunition for small-arms.
I never heard of it.
The hon. gentleman never heard of it?
No.

Why, the other night the hon. gentleman told me that Mr. Allison had negotiated a contract for
75,000,000 rounds, and then I read the statement from the Montreal Star. The Minister of Militia says that I have a thick skull and that it is difficult to penetrate my brain, and while the Minister of Militia is ordinarily very intelligent he must have been sleeping when I was making my remarks, because I was speaking of a matter entirely different from that to which he has referred.
Major-General HUGHES: I am glad to see the hon. member so much better posted than I am; I never heard of this before.

I am asking the Government to get the information and to furnish it to this House, if it is not already supplied with the information. I was stating, although probably the minister did not hear, that it is currently reported that the Government has already investigated this matter, that it has had its secret service men in the United States, and that it has ascertained the truth of the statement to which I have referred.
