' At all events, if they have not, I think the matter is of such great importance that the Government ought to get the information. They ought to do so, because of the fact, which I will repeat, that if Mr. J. Wesley Allison and the Allison Supply Co. have got themselves into the position that the Allies are compelled to engage them as middlemen for the purchase of ammunition in the United States, it is because of the credentials and standing which this Government, acting as the agents of the British Government, gave to Mr. Allison, which enabled him to go to New York and announce to

these manufacturers that he was the representative of the Canadian and British Governments and had the authority, and he alone had the authority, to negotiate for the purchase of ammunition.

I am called upon to go over this ammunition business once more for the benefit of my hon. friend. The hon. gentleman himself stated-though I had to drag it out of him-that the United States Government, which he was representing by reading from the report, paid $36.50 per 1,000 rounds last year for ammunition which they purchased from their own factories-ammunition which is cheaper to be made than ithe British Mark vii. He slipped that out gingerly and gently, and reluctantly, when I dragged it out of him-that the price was $36.50. The price that his friends, Flint & Co., asked for ammunition, was $37.50 at the lowest; their highest was $48. They came down to $37.50, but below that they would not budge-the usual commission, I presume, was the difference. The British Government made a contract on the 4th of August for 20,000,000 rounds of Mark vi. ammunition at $30 per 1,000

this, I say, is for Mark vi. ammunition, for which $25 would have been ample-the old, roundnosed ammunition, the obsolete ammunition. Some weeks after the war broke out, the contract to which I have referred was negotiated by me, assisted by Mr. Allison, and we were instrumental in bringing down the price so that the British Government saved $4.50 per 1,000 rounds of ammunition; and I challenge the world to point to one line or one word to the contrary.
I hope that what my hon. friend says is absolutely correct; I trust it is correct for the reputation and honour of this country and for the good name of the Government.
The Government does not stand any insinuations from the hon. member for St. John.

I make no insinuations; my remarks have to do with Mr. Alison and his company. But if the report in the Montreal	Star is true, and
if the profit made is the difference between $26.50 and $33, it would amount to upwards of $6,000,000. On the contract which the minister says was first made, of 75,000,000 rounds, it would amount to between $400,000 and $500,000. The hon. Minister of Militia states that he accomplished great things for the British Government. Among other things, he says that the British
Government placed an order for twenty million rounds at $30 per 1,000.
That was Mark vi. ammunition.
Which the hon. minister says is obsolete?
Yes.
That is certainly a very serious reflection upon the British War Office, and shows that they stand a long way behind the Minister of Militia in knowing what are the modern requirements.
Not necessarily. They might have appliances for making Mark vi and not for making Mark vii. I may enlighten the hon. gentleman to that extent.

At all events, does that justify this Government in standing idly by and seeing Mr. J. Wesley Allison and the Allison Supply Company taking $6.50 per thousand rounds of ammunition by way of commission out of the British taxpayer? I do not think it does. With reference to the cost of manufacture, the hon. gentleman says that the extract from the report of the Secretary of War states that manufacturers had been charging $37.50. That is true. But the Secretary of War also states that upon an order for only ten millions of rounds in their own factory, after charging up everything-which would necessarily mean all costs, including overhead charges, for otherwise the comparison would mean nothing- they were able to manufacture this ammunition at $22.50 per thousand rounds.

Then, why
did they pay their own factories $36.50?

I am citing the report
of the Secretary of War.
But I am asking the question why did they pay $36.50? And the fact that they did pay it is the fact that I dragged from the hon. gentleman, and he stated it very reluctantly.

The hon. gentleman does not do himself credit *by saying that he dragged that from me and that I stated it reluctantly. He asked me what the United States Government were paying and I said ; $37.50. About a dozen times he has stated that he dragged this from me. If he thinks that adds to the strength of his position, he is at liberty to say it as often as he pleases.

He read the
statement of cost as being only $22.50 when he knows that that did not include overhead charges.
I knew nothing of the kind. I assumed that it included everything.

He ought to
have known. Then, I dragged it from him that the only fair comparison would be with what the United States Government had paid factories;' and he was forced to admit, what he should have stated when he read his statement, that the United States Government were paying no less than $36.50 per thousand rounds a year before the war for ammunition which was Mark vi, whereas what the British Government bought W'as Mark vii.	.

No, but I have reason to suppose that the hon. gentleman has been nosing around New York.
Mr. PUGSLEY The hon. gentleman has become so familiar with matters affecting round-nosed bullets that he does not know any other suitable expression to use. I may tell him, however, that when I go to New York I do not nose around.

Slipping
around.

If my hon. friend were as anxious to preserve the honour of the country and to save money to the British treasury as he is to attack me, there would be a very easy way for him and for the Government to satisfy this committee and the people of the country that I have been entirely misinformed in this matter. That would be to produce solemn declarations from the leading manufacturers who are supplying this ammunition to the Allison Supply Company as to the amount which they are actually being paid by the Allied Governments and the amount of commission which they actually pay Mr. Allison. That would settle the matter quite easilyand in a more satisfactory way than my hon. friend can settle it by abusing me. I shall not attempt to reply to his last remarks. There may be many things in respect to the administration of the affairs of my hon. friend's department in regard to which I might follow his example and resort to abuse, but I shall not do so. This is a matter of far too great importance to justify the adoption of that attitude, and I think my hon. friend might well devote his attention to furnishing to the committee affidavits or declarations of such nature as I have indicated.

Section agreed to.
On section 2-payment of $100,000,000 may be made:

A considerable
amount of the expenditure from this vote

of credit will have relation to the cost of the concentration of troops at various points, such as Calgary, Regina, Halifax and St. John. Do I understand that the system of tender and contract will apply to such expenditures, or is this to be left to patronage committees?
The system of tender and contract will apply.

In connection with the Belgian Relief Fund, the Federal contribution has been but $50,000. Several provinces of Canada have contributed nobly to this fund, none better than my own native province. I have always felt that the sum of $50,000 contributed by the Dominion of Canada was hardly a fitting or true expression of Canadian public opinion and that something more should be done. I am still of the opinion that, notwithstanding the many demands made upon the revenues of the country, the Canadian Government, for the Canadian people, should yet do something for the relief of the destitute Belgians on a larger scale than they have heretofore done. That puts my vjew briefly before the committee, and I would like to ask the Government if they have had under consideration the matter of a further contribution to this very desirable fund.

The Government views the case of Belgium with equal sympathy and solicitude as hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House. A preliminary vote was made to that fund of $50,000. Large and wide calls were made upon the public, both in Canada, the United States and other parts of the world, which have'been most magnificently responded to. Altogether the people have given, outside of the Government contribution, a very large . sum of money and a very large amount of value in the shape of what was just as good as money to the Belgian sufferers. That flow of sympathy and active help has not been diminished in these later months, nor is it, I believe, being diminished at the present time. Belgium is suffering to-day, but she will make an equal if not greater call for help in the future. Amid all the charity and good feeling that the world has evinced in the aid of Belgium's suffering, present aid finds its *way to the comfort of the sufferers. By and by, when the war is over, Belgium will face another phase which will not appeal to the general sympathy of the world as do the sufferings of the Belgians at the present moment. She will face the situation of a

nation, a large proportion of whom are exiled from their land, and all of whose property and possessions have been either absolutely destroyed or greatly diminished by the war. There will come a time when an appeal will be made to rebuild Belgium, to make the old homes good again and to put tools and resources into the hands of the people to go back to Belgium and rebuild their ruined nation. When that time comes there will be more necessity for an appeal to Governments than there is today, because there will possibly be less general world-wide ground of appeal to charity. The Government have both of those things under consideration. They have not at all determined, quite the opposite, that the limit of what they will do on behalf of Belgium has been reached. It is a question which may well be pondered as to whether a contribution in the way of charity for the mesent is more needed than a contribution for the upbuilding of the country in a few months after this, when that country comes to be rebuilt. The whole question* is before the Government, and my hon. friend may rest assured that the heart of the Government is just as warm towards that splendid little nation and feels just as deeply its woes and sufferings as do hon. gentlemen on the other side. There is nothing but, as it were, a competition among us all as to our sympathy and good-will towards Belgium.

My hon. friend in front of me (Mr. Oliver) has suggested that the Belgians in the meantime have to eat three times a day, and that something ought to be done for them. We all hope that when the war is over the indemnity that will be collected from Germany will go to build up the ruin that has been.wrought in Belgium.
I have no doubt that this is one of the questions that will be dealt with rigorously by the Allies and that if money can repair the terrible ravages that have been made in that country it will be attended to when the indemnity is settled. I wish to join with my hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean) in saying that in my view the Dominion Government might do something more than they have done in this matter, as $50,000 does not look large enough for the Dominion of Canada to give owing to the enormous demands that have existed in Belgium during the last few months. As a matter of fact, the Dominion Government have really contributed nothing, because they have charged to the war fund $50,000

odd for carrying the Belgian Relief supplies on the Intercolonial railway. I was surprised the other day, on looking at an answer brought down by the Secretary of State in reply to a question asked by the right hon. leader of the Opposition as to the disposition of the war vote of last August, to find that among the items there is a charge for carrying the goods for the Belgian Relief by the Intercolonial railway, $50,107.25. I am informed that the Grand Trunk, the Canadian Pacific railway and the Canadian Northern railways carried these goods free of charge, and I think it extraordinary that, when the three great privately-owned railways do this free the people of Canada should have to vote out of the war vote the large amount of $50,000 to the Intercolonial railway for doing the same service. What has the Minister of Railways to say about that?

He has nothing to say. It is out of the Government's pocket anyway, and what difference does it make whether it is paid here or out of the war vote? The goods are carried through and charged up; so- what difference does it make?	.
It does not seem to me to be a proper charge against the war appropriation.

That is a matter of
opinion.
Anyway, it did not come out of the Belgians.
I did not say that.

Has any application been made to the Government for the relief of sufferers in Northern France? La France-Amerique and other associations have come to their relief, but has the Government considered doing anything? That part of France has suffered almost as much as Belgium.

I do not recall
any formal application having been made from there, or from Serbia or Poland; a.nd we must recollect that if there is any spot in the wide world where suffering is more awful than it is in any other place, you will find that place in Serbia or in some parts of Poland. If our money were only as plentiful as our hearts are sympathetic we would go to the help of all. There is this, however, to be said. France is to a large extent intact. She is a rich country, and
does not stand in quite the same position as Belgium with reference to the sufferings that have been caused in this war. I do not recall that any request has been made from Northern France, although certainly the sympathies of the people of Canada are as open to the sufferers there as to those in Belgium.
Has any suggestion been made in regard to bringing over Belgian agriculturists?

There have been statements in the papers and letters with regard to that, but I do not think it is at all practical; and for this reason. I think Belgium will want all her farmers and agriculturists in her own country when, a short period from this, she begins to rebuild.

I do not know whether the question has been asked or not, as I was not here at the beginning of the discussion, but I should like to ask if this vote of $100,000,000 will carry Canada's war expenses for the period of a year? Or, if not, for what period will it carry?

If my hon. friend had been here this morning he would have heard the statement read by the Minister of Militia. I will just give it to him in bulk. It is estimated that to carry on all the branches of this service and provide supplies for the fiscal year 1915-16, the sum of $95,475,000 will be required.

I take it, then, that this
is the measure of Canada's assistance for this year to Great Britain in this war.

No, I would not say that at all. This is what, under circumstances as they appear to us to-day, Canada is making provision for. But if in the eventualities of this war it transpires that more is required from Canada, more will be given.

I have not read this itemized statement of the Minister of Militia. But to repeat what I said in the House some time ago. I understood that the British loan of $50,000,000 or $60,000,000, which is under expenditure now, was considered to be sufficient for Canada's war expenditure on the basis of 50,000 men for a period of six months. I understand that we have or are to have in the neighbourhood of 100,000 men in the field during this coming year. As I figure it, if $50,000,000 is necessary for the establishment and upkeep of

50,000	men for six months, it will certainly take more than $100,000 000 to keep 100,000,000 men for a year. I believe that my view is sufficiently pertinent to warrant a fairly frank and full statement on the subject from the Minister of Militia or the Government.
I think my hon. friend is satisfied with the answer I gave just now.
No.

If my hon. friend wants it any stronger, will he say how much stronger he wants it? Canada is in this war to see it through, and whatever is necessary for that purpose I feel that the House will be willing to put at the disposal of the Government, and I know that the Government will do whatever is necessary. If.it requires more than this vote for the sustenance of the troops that are at present in the field or in contemplation, or if more troops are required than those now provided for, the Government will be prepared to provide those troops and those necessaries, and will depend upon the House and the country for support.

I quite appreciate that.
But I still think that the position as I placed it before the House is entitled to something more than the statement of generalities my hon. friend has offered. We are here to vote a sufficient amount of money to achieve a certain purpose. Now either we are doing it or we are not doing it; and as intelligent and responsible representatives we ougnt to know from the Government whether we are or whether we are not voting enough money to keep up our proposed establishment during the year. If we are not, we ought to know it. If we are,' it is perfectly, right for us to know. As to eventualities that may occur in the future and how they are to be met, that is another question. But the question I asked was this. If $50,000 000 will keep only 50,000 men for six months, does the Government propose to keep 100,000 men in the field for a year on $100,000,000?

The Estimates
given by the department are plain on ugh I think. They have estimated that for the fiscal year 1915-16 the amount of $95,475,000 will be required. My hon. friend need not be alarmed about it. We are now in March, and in all probability this House will meet in less than twelve months from the present time. Anything extra which needs to he provided for can be provided for. I do

not see how I can give any stronger answer than I have given, and I believe my hon. friend thinks it strong enough, hut just wants to play around it a little while.

No, if I may be pardoned, I cannot agree with my hon. friend. I will put the matter a little more definitely. What is the extent of the establishment that it is proposed to keep in the field for a year on this vote.

We have at the front at present a division, with details for filling up that division, aggregating 33,000 men, besides the Princess Patricias, consisting of 1,000 men, and 1,000 men at Bermuda. We have the second contingent at home consisting of between 22,000 and 23,000 men, including the medical and army service corps. The details of the second contingent will aggregate between 5,000 and
7,000	men. For the third Canadian contingent there have been enrolled, with details, 25,000 men, besides those we have on militia duty. Speaking of the overseas men alone, we have a total of about 90,000 men enrolled and under arms.
Are all these men under pay ?

Yes. With reference to what my hon. friend (Mr. Oliver) says, in the early part of the war, there were a great many articles and supplies procured, the use of which will extend over a part of this year, and the inclusion of these in the first estimate makes it relatively higher than this year'-s estimate, because some of these articles will be carried into the second year.

I am sorry that the information that has been given to the public so far would not indicate that my hon. friend takes a correct view of the matter. Supplies, so far from lasting into another year, have not lasted the six months of this year.

Some of them will last into the next year. For instance, the ordinary life of a wagon at the front is estimated to be less than a month. Many of our wagons and trucks will run for six months. The average life of boots and harness in the British army is six or seven weeks. Most of our boots, bad as they are, have lasted six months. It is difficult to make an absolute calculation; all we can do is to take the average life of these things in time of war, and figure on our estimates accordingly.
I think my hon. friend's allusions are hardly fortunate.
I said some of them.

The information that has been placed, before the public would indicate that the British supplies have lasted longer than- the Canadian supplies-that, in fact, an abnormally large part of the Canadian equipment has already had to be replaced by British equipment, for which, I presume, this country will be expected to pay. I do not wish to take up that side of the question; that is not what I am trying to get at. Parliament is in session, war has been in progress for eight months, and, as far as' we can see, it will continue for another year and may be much longer. What I want to arrive at is: What is the definite proposition that the Government is placing before the country ? What are we committing ourselves to ? Is the limit of Canada's aid given by this Parliament to be a vote of $100,000,000 to support a field army of
100.000	men ? If that is the fact, there is no harm in saying so. If it is not, the country, and everybody in the country, should know it. I am not calling in question the policy or decision of the Government, but I think that in all honesty and fairness they should say what their decision is.

Our intention is to keep 50,000 men in the field, which means a certain wastage every month. If it is necessary, and if it is the wish of the British Government, that we should increase that number, I presume the people of Canada will be more than willing that it shall be increased; but our figures for this vote are based upon an estimate for keeping
50.000	men in the firing line and a balance of relays going up to them. I understand that was the point of the hon. gentleman's question.
That was it.
That is what we are estimating on. If we find it our duty to give 25,000 more, I have not the slightest doubt that the people of Canada will be ready to back the Government up.

Certainly. I wanted to know what the Government's programme was. If it is to keep 50,000 men in the field with this vote of $100,000,000, we know exactly where we are, and we know the policy of the Government in regard to it. I wish.
however, to take this opportunity of, in some degree, questioning what has been done in the past in this particular. I do not-wtsh to pose as a military authority, but there are certain details of the matter that have been brought to my attention very strongly that I think the House should be made aware of, and I cannot bring these details to the attention of the House without in some measure criticizing the policy that has been pursued by the Government and the department in the past. I speak of the matter of enlistments for the contingents as they have taken place during the past months. When war was declared there was a call for men which was responded to very promptly throughout the country, and the men were sent forward. It was of course known that it was the greatest war that history had ever recorded or that might be expected to occur in the future. It was understood that Canada was to take a large part in this war, that it was to be in the war as an integral part of the Empire and was to take all the fortunes of war as they came. It was understood that there were to be further enlistments. There were posters issued, " Your King and Coun-5 p.m. try need you," and men were called upon to come forward for enlistment. In the part of the country where I live men sold their farms and their belongings on their homesteads, and came from distant parts of the West, some of them from the Peace River district, and some from far outlying homesteads, to answer this call. When they came to the centres where they expected to be enlisted, they got no consideration whatever. Many of them walked the streets, and spent the little money they had realized from the sale of their property waiting until their King and country, in the persons of the agencies of the Militia Department, should call for their service. Some of these men came in with considerable money-several hundred dollars, and some came in with very few dollars, and in a short while, as times were very dull and work was not available in the cities, many of them were stranded. Some of them were not only seriously discouraged, but had to find their way home as best they could or find some other location in which to earn a livelihood. From time to time notices came that enlistments were to be made. From time to time enlistments were made, but that condition of uncertainty and indecision continued in the conduct of the affairs of the Militia Department until some

time during the month of December, if not the month of January, when final enlistments were made for what is called the third contingent. That condition of- affairs militated very seriously against the spirit of sacrifice which is the first necessity to military enthusiasm. If a man has made every sacrifice that he can make and has placed himself at the disposal of his country and he is ignored and treated with contempt, it is not unreasonable to believe that that not only affects his military enthusiasm very seriously, but that the contagion is apt to spread and affect the enthusiasm of those in like circumstances.
I do not think I would be warranted in supporting this vote without calling the attention of the House to that condition of affairs, and to say that I consider it absolutely inexcusable. If it ever was necessary to enlist the number of men we have enlisted, and I certainly think it was necessary, it was just as necessary in the month of August last as it was in the month of January. If that enlistment of approximately 100,000 men had been made when the men were coming forward and offering themselves, it would have been an inspiration to the country at large. Although we have had a very good response, we would have, had an even better response than we have had. We might have been in a position now to have a larger force and to be more fully represented where the danger is, and where the sacrifice is being made, and where great events are to take place within the next few months. I have heard many reasons given why this was not done. It is because it was not done at the time when, in my humble judgment, it should have been done, that I approach the question as to what is the intention of the Government under the vote that is now being taken. If the Government has the intention of taking a greater part in these world-shaking events, I say to them, now is the time to take that part and not at some time in the future. If that enlistment had been made when, in my humble judgment, it should have been made, Canada would have been represented more fully than she is to-day, and it is to-day and in the next few weeks that the representation which Canada sends is wanted, and wanted most. It may be said that there was a lack of equipment, and of course equipment had to be provided, but at the same time it is necessary that men shall be gathered together, so that they may learn forms of drill, and these forms of drill could be learned in large measure without

any very full equipment. The men who could have been enlisted in August or September last would now have been ready to take their part. The equipment is ready now, but these men have not had that period of drill which fits them for their places in the firing line. They cannot go forward when the need for them is greatest, and we are prejudiced to that extent in the part we desire to take in these terrible events. It is not because of idle curiosity or a wish to criticize that I speak, but because I would not wish to see these events, which occurred in my part of the country last fall, occur in the future. I would like to see the Government make up its mind in good time exactly as to what it was going to do, and then do it, and not say: we will send our last men and spend our last dollar, and while they are saying that men are offering their services and are simply being ignored and compelled to return to their homes. If the Government purpose taking a greater part in the war than is laid down in these Estimates, now is the time to say what they intend to do, and what they want, and then let the men who are prepared to make the sacrifice know that they are wanted and that their sacrifice is appreciated.

The hon. gentleman referred to a locality in the Dominion of Canada which is unique. Edmonton is the rallying-point, so to speak, for all the country beyond it. At the outbreak of the war there were a great many splendid young fellows who had been engaged in railway construction or in one occupation or another, far beyond Edmonton, and they rallied into that city and the Edmonton regiment, under command of Colonel Maynard Rogers, which was sent to the front, was one of the best in Val-cartier or Salisbury.	Previous to my
leaving for England, it was decided that the second contingent should be enrolled. The second contingent was enrolled, and one infantry regiment was taken from Alberta, and also a cavalry regiment. Edmonton furnished a squadron, if not more, for that second cavalry regiment, and also quite a percentage of the men of the 31st regiment, which was assembled there. Immediately on my return from England, we set to work on the third contingent, and in less than three weeks from the time I recalled Colonel Griesbach, he had a lot of splendid men gathered together. There was another regiment

under Colonel Horwood. Edmonton has raised another squadron of cavalry and another regiment of infantry, all fine young fellows. It may be true that we did not take all the men offering at Edmonton, but still the enlistment had to be graduated according to the wishes and requirements expressed from time to time, and limited by our accommodation for the men. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Oliver) knows as well as I know, that Edmonton could not possibly have provided for four regiments of infantry in winter time, even if they were billeted around the town, and it is not desirable to have the men in billets if it can be avoided. Edmonton has done splendidly, but Edmonton could not possibly have accommodated several regiments, and the system of billeting out does not tend to discipline. I am satisfied that all in all Edmonton has 'done splendidly. In October when I was absent I know they wanted to go on enrolling two new regiments, but Edmonton was given a fair share, and we had to allot the proportion of enlistment fairly between the different parts of Canada. I am proud to say that the province of Alberta has furnished relatively more men per head of the population, than any other portion of the Dominion of Canada, as I believe that one out of every forty, of the people of Alberta have enrolled in the, service in one way or another. As to the city of Edmonton itself, we could not do any better than we have done. Already Alberta has, I think, supplied four regiments, a part of a fifth regiment, and six squadrons of cavalry.

I am not criticising the
Government for their conception of their duty; that is a matter for their responsibility. I merely urge that this enlistment of men for foreign service be not taken lightly. The man who leaves his farm leaves his prospects, leaves his future, even if he should return safe and sound; and for the credit of the Government and of everybody else it should be well known in good time what is wanted and when it is wanted. If this point is guarded there will be a better response and better satisfaction all round. So far as Edmonton is concerned, our position was no different from that of Calgary and many other points of the West where men came from far points expecting to be enlisted and were not enlisted. That is over and done. All I urge is that the errors or mistakes which have occurred in the past shall not occur in the 106
future. There may have been excuses for them in the past; there are no excuses for them in the future. If it is the intention of the Government that there should be a larger part taken in this war than we are preparing to take, I say now is the time and here is the place to make that declaration and that preparation.
Bill reported, read the third time, and passed.

On motion of Hon. Frank Cochrane (Minister of Railways and Canals), Bill No. 105, to amend the Government Railways Act and to authorize the purchase of certain railways, was read the second time, and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Blain in the Chair.
On section 1-acquisition of railways and works:

I was not here on Saturday when this Bill was up. I would like to renew the question I asked on another occasion:	Is there any intention to take
over the Quebec and Oriental and the Atlantic, Quebec and Western railways.

I do not think it is
in the interest of the country that I should name any roads that I propose to take over.
The International has been taken over?

Yres, and this Bill is
to ratify that action.

And the minister is not in a position to state what intends to do with regard to those other roads?
. Mr. COCHRANE: Not yet.
The minister provides in this Bill for taking over two railways. Can he tell us about these roads?
I explained that the other day.
I regret to say I was not here.

The International road runs from Campbellton to St. Leonard's, a distance of 112 miles. It is in good physical condition, except for one curve and grade, which I think we shall be able to change. I have a vote of $25,000 this year to do it. The justification for taking over this road is that the International bridge at St. Leon-



ard's was being completed and it would have enabled this road to cut into the Intercolonial railway's trade. That place is a very large lumber section, and the taking over of this road will give us a shorter line through the eastern states. They could have injured the receipts of the Intercolonial railway very much. We shall be able to serve the shippers at that point at a lower rate and, I think, make as much in net profits for the Intercolonial railway as we could the other way. The other road, the New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island, is taken over for the purpose of connecting the Intercolonial railway with the car ferry for Prince Edward Island. That is a road thirty-six miles long not in very good shape.
Is that the road a part of which is floating?
No. I was over it, and while it was not exactly in good condition we have improved it to some extent and must improve it more.
How much are we giving for it?

It is stated in the Bill -$270,000. It was bought on condition that we pay four per cent until the House voted the money to pay for it. The other road was leased for five years at $90,000 a year, which is a little less than 3i per cent, and then we are buying it at $2,700,000. I think I can safely say that it would cost at least that amount to build the road to-day; I think it would cost that when it was built.
What has been the result of the operation of the International railway ? What information can the minister give as to the receipts and expenditures ?
I cannot give the exact receipts, but I think I can safely say that the road is paying its running expenses.

Has the minister given any consideration to the construction of a bridge at Campbellton, over the Restigouche river, to connect the International and Intercolonial systems with the system of railways in the Gaspe peninsula ? Numerous petitions have been sent in by the people of Restigouche, the board of trade of the town of Campbellton, the county council of the county of Restigouche, the town of Dal-housie, and all the municipalities on both sides of the river. The late Government was petitioned in this matter, and petitions have been sent to the present Administration. I understand that a deputation was I Mr. Cochrane.]
here recently 'in connection with the matter. Has the minister given any consideration to the subject ?
I have not considered it.

I am glad indeed to hear the minister express the opinion that this traffic can be carried by the shorter route over the International railway across the bridge which is now being constructed over the St. John river. I am informed by the president of the company that the bridge will be ready for use by April 15. Certainly it is creditable to the company that, having begun the work only in the month of August last, they have been able to complete it in such a short period of time. The construction of the bridge is also somewhat unique by reason of the fact that no public aid has been given to the company either by this Government, the Provincial Government or the municipalities. This shows the great confidence which the people interested in the traffic have in the possibilities of that traffic. I know the country very well; the railway runs through a magnificent country, which is well timbered, and a large part of which is 'veil adapted to agriculture. Since the construction of the road I understand that over 5,000 settlers have gone into that country.
Into the timber land?

Thej have gone into the timber country, settling along the railway line, but very great care is being exercised, both by the railway authorities and by the Government to prevent the destruction of the timber. As I say, the land is exceedingly fertile and well adapted to farming, and I am sure that before many years it will become a splendid agricultural country. I quite realize that the Government has acted wisely in taking the road over. I have always felt, from the statements of railway experts, that this line occupies a strategical position, and if it were to go into the hands of another company interested in taking the traffic, the result would be a serious interference with the traffic handled by the Intercolonial railway. I am glad, indeed, that the minister has decided to take the road over. I think that if he acts under the powers contained in the first section as prudently, so far as the company is concerned, as he has acted in respect of these two roads, the country will not be very
much the	loser	by	reason of	thislegislation.	I desire	to express	mygratification	that	at last, after many	years in	which	the	acquisition	of
branch lines of the Intercolonial railway has been urged by members of this House, more especially, [DOT] I think, on this side-until some four years ago, when the hon. member for Kings and Albert (Mr. Fowler) took the matter up-to know that we are likely at last to have a consummation of the policy of taking over the branch lines of the Intercolonial railway. If I were in my hon. friend's position, however, I would not be too careful to be always sure that the branch lines would pay the Intercolonial from the standpoint of traffic.

You have just said
that if I buy the others upon as good terms as I bought these, I should be doing all right.

That is true; that would be as to price. But there are some small branch lines which do not show very great traffic earnings, but which serve fairly important sections of the country. When it becomes known that, by reason of Government operation, there will be a permanent, continuous and satisfactory service, industries will be established along these lines, and the country will develop to a greater extent than it possibly could develop while uncertainty of operation exists. Another important matter is that instead of being obliged to pay double rates, as they do now, persons who receive goods, over the railway will be subject to the very great advantage of only one freight charge, based on mileage. I feel sure that the carrying out of this policy will' result in a very great benefit to the people of the Maritime Provinces, and I think also to certain sections of the province of Quebec. .

When the International railway was built there was to be a bridge at each end of the road, one at St. Leonard's, and one over the Restigouche river at Campbellton. An Act of Parliament was passed authorizing the construction of a railway and highway bridge over the Restigouche river, for the purpose of giving the Gaspe peninsula easy access to the Intercolonial railway and the New England States.
Was an appropriation made?

A subsidy was voted, but the president of the railway, Mr. Malcolm, subsequently declared that this subsidy was not sufficient to build the line, and that the Government would have to guarantee the bonds. This subject was under consideration when the change of Administration 1061
took place. However, the taking over of the International will provide a short cut to the New England States for the Gaspe peninsula. The Quebec Oriental railway was known at different times by two other names. It was originally known as the Baie des Chaleurs railway; then it had another name, the' Atlantic and Lake Superior; finally it became the Quebec Oriental railway. When the minister takes over this road I am sure that he will see that the properties which have been taken over as rights of way will be paid for. Many farmers from Matapedia to New Carlisle have had their farms cut up by the construction of this road, and have never been paid for the right of way. The station at Cross point, opposite Campbellton, is on the farm of a man named Fraser-, who never received a dollar for his property. The Baie des Chaleurs Railway Company made certain offers which the farmers would not accept. When the company went into insolvency, the Atlantic and Lake Superior Company took over the project, and they also did not pay for the right of way. There are, in addition, claims for labour, board and material on the part of persons all along the line from Matapedia to New, Carlisle. I hope that the minister will see that the people are treated properly; that those who gave their properties as rights of way, and those who furnished material, board, etc., are properly indemnified I would call his attention also to the importance of the lower part of the road-the new road which has been built from New Carlisle to Gaspe. That is in as good . condition as the International was or is to-day. A special subsidy was voted by this Parliament for the erection of some 25 bridges over a very difficult country down the Gaspe basin. The fact that this road is in good condition brings about a peculiar condition of affairs. At Chandler, in the township of Pabos, in Gaspe, an American company from Philadelphia has established a large pulp industry and is expending $2,000,000 or $3,000,000. I understand that a number of Canadians are now associated with that company. This company transported a lot of their material over the Atlantic and Lake Superior railway from the Intercolonial at Matapedia down over the Quebec and Eastern to New Carlisle, from Matapedia to New Carlisle being so unsatisfactory, they have entered into an agreement with Air. Scholes to utilize the deep water wharf at Gaspe to bring in supplies to Gaspe, which is connected with the Atlantic, Quebec and Western railway;
commons
and then they move their materials to Chandler over that road, which is in a good state, so that the Intercolonial is avoided entirely and loses all this traffic because of the state of the railway between the Intercolonial and the new Gaspe railway. I hope when the minister considers that the time has come-and it surely has come-when Gaspe should have proper connection with the Intercolonial, he will bear these points in mind. Gaspe is the oldest constituency in Quebec; it was there that Jacques Cartier stopped before he ever went to Quebec or Montreal; and the people there have been looking in vain for proper railway accommodation, and I trust the minister will see that they get it and get it under favourable terms. I trust he will also see that all the claims which the people have been seeking to recover, year in and year out, for the last 20 years will be paid-claims for time checks, right of way, board bills-, and accounts of various kinds. When the road is taken over, let us hope that this chapter will be finally closed to the satisfaction of the population in that district.

When the time comes for taking over the road, I will certainly make that :a condition. Whether it is mortgaged up to the teeth or not, if they want to sell it to us they will have to pay these debts. I had a man go down to try to get a statement of the debts from the people themselves, and I think he now has it pretty fully prepared. In reference to the other point, as long as people can get shipping by water it is very hard for any railway to compete; but I can understand that if this branch of the road were put in proper order and this connection made by building the bridge so as to provide a line to the eastern States that way, we might possibly capture some traffic. I will certainly have the matter looked into. Financial conditions are such that we cannot do much this year, but that will not prevent us investigating and being ready when the time comes.

I notice the words:
Provided further no such railway shall be so constructed, leased, purchased or otherwise acquired unless it directly connects with the then existing Government railway system.

That might prevent
what my hon. friend is talking about. These two roads are owned by two different people.

Yes, two different roads
connecting at New Carlisle-one 100 miles in length and one 102 miles in length.

They are too long and
do not absolutely connect. What is the definition of "directly"? Suppose a railway were on one side of the St. Lawrence river and the Government railways were on the other side and you had a railway ferry across, would that be direct connection?
It might be, but not unless the ferry was there.
Take the city of Quebec. They have a ferry on which they take cars across. Would a railway starting in Quebec be considered as being in direct connection with the Intercolonial?
There might be a point there.

I shall make it plainer. It has been stated in Montreal during the past week that certain railway arrangements have been made satisfactorily to the Government to do something with the Quebec and Montmorency railway-that the railway is going to be put in better condition and possibly pass into other hands. Under this section, if that railway ferry makes direct connection with the Intercolonial, that road could be taken over under this Act. What is the length of .that road?
It is about 90 odd miles long.
It would depend altogether on what is meant by direct connection.

Before the tunnels were built under the Detroit river my hon. friend would not say that the Grand Trunk and Canadian Pacific railway did not have direct connection between the two sides of the river. I am not arguing in reference to the road referred to, because I have not considered it.
I rather agree with the minister that that might be taken as a direct connection. Consequently this road might be taken over under this particular Act.
I think not.
Has any suggestion been made that this road will be taken over?
No.

It is a matter of some interest in Montreal. It was being dis-

cussed quite freely there the other day, and many business men in Montreal who were stockholders in this road were led to believe that it was going to be taken over.
It has not come to me anyway.	-

I understood
the other day that the Government policy was that this legislation was to apply only to branches of the Intercolonial.
Yes.

Section agreed to.
On section 3-to authorize the purchase of the New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island railway:

I would like to express, on behalf of the people of that section of Westmorland county, gratification that the Government has seen fit to enter into an agreement for the purchase of the New Brunswnck and Prince Edward Island railway. That is a branch line of railway that has been operated by a company for some thirty years from	Sackville to Cape
Tormentine, and during that time it has been allowed to get into a rather dilapidated condition, as the minister has said. It runs through settlements where there is quite a large traffic from lumber as well as from the agricultural community, and it also connects some rather thriving villages with the junction at Sackville. I am sure the people of that district will appreciate very much the fact that the Government is going to take over this road and make it part and parcel of the Intercolonial. I would urge on the minister that it is very necessary during the coming -season to improve the road. If we are going to have the car ferry across to the island, this road will require many improvements immediately. I believe that the road has been under operation by the Government since August 1st last. The only criticism I would offer would be that, unfortunately for the people living along a section of that road, the Government, since taking it over, have increased the freight rates. I do not think the company ran the road at a loss, and I cannot understand why it was necessary for the Government to increase the freight rates as high as 100 per cent in some cases. I should like the minister to look into the matter and see if he cannot put the rates back to what they were when the road was -operated by the company.
I shall be very glad to look into it.

Section agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time, and passed.
At six o'clock, the House took recess.
The House resumed at eight o'clock. SUPPLY.
The House in Committee of Supply, Mr. Blain in the Chair.
Department of Railways and Canals-Intercolonial railway-Chaudi6re Junction to St. Romuald-double tracking, $30,000.
What is that for?

speakeroldname: Hon. FRANK COCHRANE (Minister of Railways and Canals):
speechtext:
We are doubletracking there. The contract was let to Soper and McDougall, and this is a re-vote of $30,000 to complete the contract.
Intercolonial railway-diversion of line between Nelson and Derby Junction, $6,000.

When the committee rose on Friday night, I had been referring the minister to the matter regarding the taking up of the rails on the south side of the Miramichi river and drawing his attention to the fact that the residents of that section of my county, who had enjoyed the privilege of a railway for some thirty or forty years, were still without an approach to the railway on the north side of the river. I intimated that the minister had made some promise regarding this matter last year. I find that it was not the minister who made the promise but the acting minister, the hon. Minister of Customs (Mr. Reid). Let me refer to the debate on that occasion as reported in Hansard, 1914, page 5112.
Mr. Loggie:	The minister on Friday last
said that:
" Bridges are now being built across the river, or it is intended to build them."
Who is intending to build them?
Mr. Pugsley:	He was more positive last
week than he is now.
Mr. Reid:	No. I,am just as positive nbw
that the bridges are to be built.
Then, on page 5113:
Is it not reasonable that, before final action is taken, the Minister of Railways and Canals should discuss the matter with the Provincial Government and see what is advisable to be done, whether this Government or the Provincial Government should build the bridges and where they should be located? That is the reason why it is very difficult for me to give definite information upon the matter or to arrive at a final decision.
Who led them to believe that?
I would judge it was the Minister of Railways and Canals.
I would like the hon. gentleman to prove it.

I cannot do any more than give the statement of the hon. member for St. John as quoted here and confirmed by my hon. friend from Gloucester (Mr. Tur-geon), who is reported at page 5113 to have said:
I remember the occasion when the Minister of Railways and Canals told the people of the locality that he proposed to take away that railway because it was, in his estimation, not a paying propositon, and that in compensation for the railway facilities he was taking away he would build a bridge, or two bridges -one for sure-across the river In order that the people might have connection between their homes and the station.
Let me just say now that I never made that promise nor led them to believe any such thing.

Of course, I have to take what the minister says, but at the same time I think that the deputy minister and tlje acting minister a year ago did encourage me to believe that the matter would be favourably considered.
Not in what you have read.

Well, I do not know. The hon. Minister of Customs said:
I am just as positive now that the bridges are to be built.
He did not say by whom.
Who was he speaking for?
I do not know whom he was speaking for.

I do not want to get into any controversy with my worthy friend the Minister of Railways and Canals; what I want him to do is to implement what I look upon as his promise. The minister has made a survey of the very places where the bridges are to be constructed. I want him to tell me if he can, what is the estimated cost of the substructures. Even if the local government should build the substructure, I am sure that his department will not object to supplying the superstructure, because they have old bridge material almost going to waste that would admirably suit this situation. The Government are not doing their duty to that locality, inasmuch as they have removed the railway, if they do not give these people an approach to the railway that they are now operating. The people of that portion of my county have been encouraged to believe that there would be a bridge built there and that they would have an approach to the railway that is being operated. I do not think that this Government should begrudge the money that it will take, and I hope they will take the matter into consideration and have the bridge constructed even if the local government pays the cost of the substructure. It would not be a very large outlay. The people whom they have deprived of the railway that they had been enjoying for so many years are surely deserving of consideration in this matter. I know the minister wants to be fair. The people were led to believe that these bridges would be constructed.
If the minister is not in favour of doing the entire work himself, he should at least implement the promise made by the acting minister last year, and supply the superstructure if. the local government would build the substructure. This is a very urgent matter, from my point of view, and I know I am stating the mind of my constituents when I press it upon the minister.

I made an inspection of this branch and I found there would have to be two new bridges erected and that the road was not in a fit state to run trains upon. The service was not good on the road, and I found that most of the people going to Chatham and Newcastle crossed over the river and took the railway on the

other side. I did not consider there was traffic enough to warrant us going to the large expenditure necessary to put that road in proper shape. I do not want to have the hon. gentleman put words in my mouth, and I may tell him I never led the people to believe anything of the kind he says I did. I consulted Mr. Maloney, the mill-owner, and I asked him if we fixed the road and ran trains on it would he give us his traffic, and his reply was that if it suited him he would, but that if he could ship by boat he would do so. I do not blame him at all for it, because, of course, he was quite right, but the fact remained that there was not enough traffic on the road to justify its operation. I repeat that I did not give the people down there the promise that the hon. gentleman says I gave them. When I go on a special trip I have my secretary by me who makes a note of anything said by delegations, and consequently I am able to speak quite definitely on such matters as that. Sometimes the Federal Government may contribute to an interprovincial bridge, but it certainly is not the policy to contribute to bridges within the province. If our Highways Bill ever passes, we can take up the very kind of thing to which the hon. gentleman refers, because this may be one of the highways which it would be in the general interest to build. My hon. friend (Mr. Loggie) shakes his head, but he never yet has heard the scheme described which might be evolved from that measure, had it passed.
1 am not bringing that Bill in now, however, and there is no use in discussing it. I know nothing of surveys having been made, as the hon. gentleman says they were, but perhaps the work was done when I was away, and, therefore, I .cannot contradict my hon. friend. It is the province which should move in the matter and not this Government, and if the province sees its way to undertake any bridges which this Government might assist them in, I shall be glad to hear representations from the province in that respect.
Intercolonial railway-diversion of line between North Sydney and Leitche's Creek, $60000.
What has been the increase in the freight rates from Sydney, on account of the construction of that line?
I do not know; I have not the freight rates here.

This line is of course a great accommodation to the people of
Sydney Mines and Bras d'Or, but the freight rates have been very much increased since it was constructed, as I have been informed by business men in Sydney.

The matter has not
been brought to my attention and I will look into it at once. As it would appear now there does not seem to be justification for it.
Neither do I think there is any justification for the increase, and I would be glad if the minister would makq a note of it and inform me.
I will.

I am informed that the same freight rates are charged from Truro to Sydney, as from Antigonish to Sydney, although there is a difference in the haul of eighty miles. Does the hon. minister think that is fair?

It would depend on
where the shipment comes from. I do not think it would be fair as regards local shipments, because I think there should be a somewhat higher charge for an extra haul of 80 miles.

I have been informed by a gentleman who was about to buy a horse at Truro, that the freight rate quoted to him for the carriage of that horse to Sydney was $7.20. He bought the horse in Antigonish, 80 miles away, and he had to pay a rate of $7.20. I do not think it is fair to the railway itself or to Antigonish and the points intervening between Truro and Sydney, that the same rates should be charged.
You say that the rate on a horse from Antigonish to Sydney was the same as from Truro to Sydney?
Yes.
Can you give me particulars as to the shipment?
The shipper.was Ronald AlcKeegan of Catalone Gut, Cape Breton county, and the waybill was dated January 20, No. 243, car 60460.

I will inquire about
that.
Intercolonial Railway-general protection of highways, $16,000.
This vote includes: Subway at Amherst, $9,000; subway west of Little Metis, $7,010.
Is the one at Moncton finished ?
No.
How many level crossings have been done away with on the Intercolonial railway ?
My official says that 20 have been done away with since I took office.

Some years ago an Act was passed for the elimination of level crossings. The Board of Railway Commissioners have power to recommend that a certain amount of the cost be paid by the municipalities, a certain amount by the Government and a certain amount by the road. The Intercolonial railway, as a Government road, should set a good example to the provincial municipalities in the matter of getting rid of level crossings.

I wish to call the minister's attention to the matter of calling for tenders for the coal- supply for the year. In a great many of the mines in Nova Scotia the men are working half time, and they are very anxious to know when the coal contracts are to be let. For years these contracts have always been let'at this time of the year, and I cannot see any reason why the minister should postpone the matter unduly. The department is a month late in asking for tenders;
I should like to know the reason for the delay.

We have a large quantity on hand; that is why we have been slow in calling for tenders. As the hon. gentleman knows, I have been exceedingly busy this winter I am isorry to say that my deputy has -been sick nearly all winter, and my secretary, part of the time. Consequently, I have had more work to do than I would have had if these officials had been with me.

This matter would be reported upon by the management of the Intercolonial railway; they know how much coal they have on hand, and can estimate how much they will need. The calling for tenders is a matter that should be settled early in the season, particularly -this year, when navigation is somewhat difficult and vessels hard to get. Then, again, there is the question in which the men are interested: As to how much work they are going to be guaranteed this year. They are working half time in many of

the coal mining districts, and complaints aie coming from the representatives of the men in regard to the matter.
Mr. COCHRANE; It will not be long before we take the matter up.
Intercolonial railway-Halifax, docks and wharves, $30,000.
This is to finish up pier No. 2.
It has nothing to do with the real terminal scheme?

No.
Mr. A. K. MACLEAN': Could the minister give me an explanation of a somewhat large amount which is in the Supplementary Estimates for Halifax docks ? Has that reference to the ocean terminals?
This was carried on from last year and has been put in the Supplementary Estimates. This f30,000 completes pier No. 2.
This is for No. 2 pier? Mr. COCHRANE: Yes.
Have all the land damages been settled in Halifax?

I do not think there were any land claims in connection with this work. On the big scheme they are not settled, by any means.
Intercolonial railway-Halifax, new terminal facilities, $3,000,000.

How much does the Government expect to spend to complete the terminals there?
Mr. COCHRANE That would be a little hard to say. The road down to the docks, the station, the sea wall, 2,000 feet long and the slip, have to be completed. The breakwater is well under way.
How much will be spent this year?
I suppose when these terminals are completed they will have sufficient capacity to accommodate all railways that may go in there?
Yes, that is the idea.
I suppose the Canadian Northern railway will eventually get there ?

They have been discussing the question of obtaining running

rights or arranging for an interchange of traffic in the province of Quebec.

In reference to the guarantee of bonds, I think there is embodied in one of our statutes a provision whereby the Intercolonial may enter into some arrangement to this end with the Canadian Northern. So they will have to get there in some way to complete their lines. There are the 'Canadian Northern railway, the Transcontinental, the Canadian Pacific railway, and the Intercolonial railway.
Yes.
I understand that these terminals are of sufficient capacity to accommodate all the traffic that will come to Halifax?

When the whole
scheme is laid out it will accommodate all the roads that will come in for a number of years. But I do not know that the works that are now under contract will do that.
This is only one unit?
Yes.

And I suppose the
Government is keeping in its own hands the right to regulate the terms made with these other roads coming in?
Yes.
This being Government property, and the Intercolonial railway having possession, the other .railways will come in under approximately the same terms?
\es.

That being the case, if traffic increases as it ought to increase, I think the Government is not making much of a mistake in going a little ahead of the traffic. By letting the contract for one unit, and with plans for others, I imagine the Government will be able to keep up with the traffic as it increases.
Yes.

The point I ask definitely is this-will the right of all railways be protected? Outside of the Intercolonial railway, will the other roads be brought in on practically equal terms, so that one will not have an advantage over the other?

Everybody will be
treated alike.
I suppose the country is committed a little more to the National Transcontinental than to the other lines?
Something similar to the Intercolonial railway itself.
So that the Intercolonial railway will be the Government end of the Transcontinental ?
Yes.

Of course, the sum is a large one to expend, especially this year, when dollars look much larger than they do when revenues are buoyant. But, personally, I should think the Government is taking the right stand in preparing for future traffic, and, while having plans for extension, to complete only one unit. We shall be disappointed in this country if we do not have traffic enough going to our maritime ports to use the greater portion of these facilities.

The whole new
scheme covers accommodation for thirty boats at one time.
That will be three units.
Yes.

To be finished only as
trade increases?
Yes.
Has the department under immediate consideration the proposal to connect the railway system at Dartmouth and the railway system on the Halifax side with a bridge?

We have not done
any more than talk it over; we have not done anything practically. I have been wmiting to find out if there is enough traffic on that new Dartmouth-Deans road to make it worth while. I am not familiar enough with the country there to know what the traffic is likely to be.

You are not likely to
make an early commencement on that project?	-
Not this year.

If members of the Government come to Halifax within the next few months and make statements about the early construction of this bridge, I shall be justified in saying that they are unofficial and unjustified?
I have made my statement, and I cannot help what others may say.
When the station at the south end is open, is it intended to close the north station?

I think likely that
station will be closed, but we shall have to keep our facilities for freight there. I do not see the necessity for two stations.
There was a disagreement at one time between the Intercolonial railway and another railway about the use of our station in Halifax.
The Halifax and Southwestern .

Something of that kind.
Did that ever get straightened out?

No, they owe us quite a sum. We are trying not to let them get in any deeper.
Intercolonial railway-Halifax-to increase accommodation and provide machinery at, $3,500.
Does that mean shops at Halifax?

It means some track
changes there.
Intercolonial railway-Halifax-Willow Park sewer, $14,900.

This sewer emptied
where the new harbour facilities are being provided, and we had to change the outlet.

I see the Government
spent $100 there last year.
That was for a survey. The contract was not let then.
Do you intend to spend it all this year?

We will have to, I
think.
Intercolonial railway-Hampton-subway and facilities at, $39,750.
This is a re-arrangement of the tracks to provide proper switching facilities; also the subway will eliminate a dangerous crossing.
You did not spend much on that last year,

No, we shut down on nearly everything last year.
Intercolonial railway-installation of block system in connection with operation, $14,000.

I am sure it would be
of interest to the public to know how much of the line is under the block system. And does the minister use any of these signals that we see advertised? I know that gentlemen waited on the department to have

danger signals introduced connected with the block system.

I do not know what
system my hon. friend refers to. Anything of that kind that is brought to my notice, I refer to the engineers on the ground, because they .know about these things and I do not. The people in this case are the General Railway Signal Company of Canada, Limited, of Lachine, Que. The portions of the road under the block signal system are from St. John to Hampton; Moncton to Painsec Junction, and Windsor Junction to Halifax. These are the three most crowded portions of the line.
How many miles altogether? Will the minister make inquiry about that?
Yes.

Without attempting to claim credit, I may say that in discussing railway matters, particularly in the province in which I live, I try to make the situation of the Intercolonial railway clear even since my hon. friend the present minister has mixed it up. I have endeavoured to point out to the people in the other provinces that the Intercolonial railway was not the drag that they had sometimes been led to believe, but that it was a good piece of property.
I believe that.

And I have tried to do that no matter which Government was in power, in defence of our own Government railways, because I believe that the Inter- ' colonial railway has been largely misunderstood for many years and that the money we have been putting into it "has not been sunk but will bring a return. I want this information so that in discussing the Inter-[DOT]colonial as a national undertaking, a national property, I can tell the people how many miles are run on the most modern block system. I think it would be well if I could have that information.

I shall have that information to-morrow. If I had a time-table I could at once give the distances. This is to finish the sections which are now being equipped in this way.
Intercolonial railway-installation of telephone system in connection with operation $100,000.
What is this installation of a telephone system?

It ia for a telephone system between Moncton and Ste. Rosalie Junction. The most modem way of operating a railroad is by telephone; it is considered much safer. Only part of this Was spent last year. I hope to complete the work this year.
Is it the intention to install this all over the line in time?
As soon as we can.
The Government will own this telephone system?

Unfortunately our station at Levis was burned last fall. We want to change it around, and will have to buy a little property. We hope to secure better accommodation both for the ferry and for the town.
Is this sum all for the improvement of the station?

The station and the additional land we have to buy-facilities in connection with the station.
Intercolonial railway-Moncton locomotive and power shops, with equiimient, $110,000.

This is a big jump from Levis to Moncton, jumping over Riviere du Loup. I do not see why there is nothing for Riviere du Loup in this estimate. Is the minister ready to tell me what he intends to do for Riviere du Loup this summer?
You mean in connection with the track from the proposed wharf?
I should like to know what the minister has in mind to do for Riviere du Loup, and then I shall have some questions to put. .

I do not think there
is anything in the Estimates for it.

There is $50,000 in
the Public Works Estimates for improvement of the harbour. If I am not mistaken, last year the Minister of Railways and Canals was ready to help the "Public Works Department in connection with the unloading of coal at Riviere du Loup for the Intercolonial railway. Is there any prospect that next summer something will be done by the
Minister of Railways to help the Public Works Department in that scheme?

There has been a development of coal in New Brunswick and the policy of the Intercolonial has been changed to some extent in consequence. We feel that we can buy coal in New Brunswick as cheaply as we can buy it in Nova Scotia, and I understand that we can deliver it cheaper from New Brunswick than we could get it done by boats, as we would have to rail it up from the station. Our coal at Levis, for instance, costs us more than coa.' costs the Grand Trunk or Canadian Pacific railway at Montreal, as our facilities are not what they should be, and it takes us much longer to unload, and they charge demurrage. Taking into consideration everything,
I do not think there would be enough coal brought to Riviere du Loup to warrant our expending $75,000 or $100,000 to install an unloading plant. I think we could better afford to bring the coal from New Brunswick.
Do I understand that the minister has abandoned the plan to have coal unloaded at Riviere du Loup.
Yes.
Then the Department of Public Works are to proceed alone with the scheme for the improvement of the harbour.
As far as we are concerned, I have given my explanation.
Will the minister explain what it is proposed to do at Moncton? Is this an extension of the present dock?
It is the installation of a power plant, and of new equipment and a rearrangement of the machinery. I do not think it is for increased buildings so much as for increased power.
You have not been building cars to any extent at Moncton?
Only in slack times.

Is it the intention to build
more cars at Moncton?

That policy has not
been decided, because 1 am told the cars cost more than we can buy them for, although I do not know that that is a good reason for not building them. We are short of power down there, and w^nt to increase it. No matter who runs the Transcontin-

ental railway, we must have a good deal of work there. There is not much of a shop in connection with the Transcontinental there. But even for our own work we have not enough power there at present.
Is that for new buildings?
It is part of the power scheme, and for rearranging the equipment.
It says " locomotive and car shops ". Is the Government building any locomotives there?

No, we never have
done so.
I think the Government has built some refrigerator cars, vans and that sort of thing down there. The Government has never tried to build passenger cars there?
Only second-class. We have ordered some steel this year to see how they can work down there.

This question has often
been discussed before, but I know it is not easy to work out. Owing to the greater speed at which things go nowadays, railways and everything else, some of the larger companies are trying to do away with their wooden cars and use all-steel cars instead. Are we having steel cars made for the Intercolonial railway?

We have steel frames. Our wooden cars, when they go to the United States, get mixed up with steel cars there, and when they get home enormous repairs have to be made. We shall have to cut them out altogether in future and not run them over there at all. We are making steel-frame freight cars now.

Has the Government
purchased any passenger cars recently?

We are buying twelve this year; some of steel, and some of steel finished in wood. We are buying some of each to see how they work out. The allsteel cars cost about $250 apiece more than the steel-and-wood cars.
Intercolonial railway-Moncton-elimination level crossings and grades, $125,000.
Is this to de.al with the crossing on Main street, Moncton?

This is to finish the
one they are working at now. The contract has already been let.
A return I got the other day showed that the contract price "'as $45,000, I think.

I have the particulars here: Subway superstructure, $21,000; substructure, $63,100 ; 4,500 sq. yards paving, $15,750; supporting track, 2,500 lin. feet, $1,120; 26,500 ft. b.m. hard pine, $1,590; 2,000 lbs. iron in trestle, $60; labour placing girders, $200; concrete platform and baggage room floor, $9,000. There are several other items, so my hon. friend will see there is a tremendous lot of work to do besides the excavation for which the contract has been let.
Was my hon. friend reading from the contract that has been let, or was that the estimate?
The estimate is that it will take $125,000 to finish up the whole thing. The contract that has been let is not for the whole work.	*
The $45,000 relates to the contract that has been let.
Yes, the total cost. There will have to be some change made around the station; otherwise we shall have to spend a great deal more money.
Is it the intention of the department to eliminate the crossings just a little beyond the city?

that scheme is being worked out. I think an arrangement has been made with the Moncton council. I am not very familiar with it, but I think it is settled that we are to change the whole thing. Several crossings have to be attended to, but we are not going on with them this year because we cannot get the money.
This $125,000 is necessary to complete that?
Yes, and what other changes are necessary?
Has the minister decided whether to ask for tenders for this work, or is the railway going to do it?

I have not considered that yet.
Intercolonial railway, Monoton-installation of roofing, $22,500.

The cement roof down there gave us a great deal of trouble in the winter season. It sweats and drops down on the machinery and the men. We had to take it up in instalments and put

insulated roofing underneath.

This is a matter which
affects my constituency, and it is only fair that 1 should say that I have been following it with the greatest care. It was proposed in the first instance, after a conference between the Government and the Dominion Coal Company, that a spur line should be built to the town of Wallace.

And I contend that, where you have the capital, the land and the facilities work should be concentrated. It would be of great advantage to the city of Moncton and to the surrounding country as well. I know myself that there are a large number of men who are experts in the car-building business, having been working in the near-by town of Amherst. My hon. friend from Cumberland (Mr. Rhodes) will bear me out in saying that there is no work for these men, and that if

they could be occupied at their own calling they would be able to build ears at Moncton, I believe, as cheaply as those cars could be purchased elsewhere. We shall have the same expense for upkeep, and the foremen, general managers and officials of the Intercolonial railway could oversee a great deal more work than is being done at the city of Moncton now. I cannot see any reason why cars cannot be built in the city of Moncton as cheaply as they can be built elsewihere; I am sure that our working people as well as those dependent on the trade coming from working people, would appreciate the efforts of the department very much.
