I do not wish to claim the attention of the committee at any length, but I cannot sit quietly in my place and hear the hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. Copp) figure out that, in view of the fact that industrial conditions are very quiet in the neighbouring constituency of Cumberland, and men there are out of employment, they should be given employment in the constituency of Westmorland. Rather, I take it, the argument would be that the Government should contract for the construction of cars in the town of Amherst. I note my hon. friend's admission that he does not know anything about railways. I think he is quite right; and I will admit the same with regard to myself.	With us as participants, the
discussion would be largely academic, and I	do not	feel that	we
should take up the time of , the committee. But when we discuss the advantage of constructing cars in Westmorland, I am sure that the hon. gentleman, knowing the conditions, will admit that while a corporation or group of individuals might construct cars in Moncton as well as elsewhere the Government employees, under conditions that exist in Moncton, could not construct them as cheaply.
Why?

The hon. gentleman need not cross-question me. But if he were frank, and had in mind the public interest rather than the interest of his own candidature, he would admit that conditions in the Government works at Moncton are such as not to call for the greatest efficiency in construction. The policy of large railway cor

porations in Canada and the United States in recent years has been to get away from the construction of rolling stock and to content themselves entirely with the repairs of such rolling stock as happens to be out of repair on their lines. They find that they can purchase cars in the open market from companies that make a specialty of manufacturing cars, more cheaply than they can manufacture them, having regard to the circumstance that the manufacture of cars by their own corporation would be, at best, only a side line and they would not be able to make a specialty of it as would a company peculiarly in the car construction business.
If the hon. gentleman wishes me to suggest some method whereby the condition of unemployment in his neighbouring constituency may be remedied at the tnoment, I would say that perhaps the best method to pursue would be to make a contract for the manufacture of cars in the town of Amherst.

With a view to settling the dispute which seems to have arisen between two hon. gentlemen as to where these cars should be built, I would suggest to the minister that the cars be constructed in the city of Charlottetown. We have in that city one of the best equipped shops that can be found in America, and we have a large number of skilled workmen who are well adapted to the work of building cars. Furthermore, we have just as much right to have those cars constructed in Prince Edward Island as these hon. gentlemen have to have them constructed in either of their respective constituencies. These hon. gentlemen assume to have a monopoly of the whole Intercolonial railway from Sydney to Montreal. One would think that the hon. member for Westmorland and the hon. member fir Cumberland control the whole thing, and that no one else should have a show; that the cars should not be built anywhere except in their constituencies. I would ask the hon. minister to take my suggestion into serious consideration.

My attention was particularly drawn to this matter when I saw in the press of Amherst a report that the town council held a special meeting not long ago to consider what they were going to do with the unemployed in Amherst, and the suggestion was made that the local Government give assistance to the town of Amherst in order to provide employment during the period of hard 107
times. It was only as a matter of kindness that I suggested that the men be taken to Moncton and be given profitable employment so that they should not be thrown on the mercies of their town or province. It is not a matter between myself and the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Rhodes). I do not say that the problem could be solved at once, but I do think that the Government should make the experiment. The cars can be built at Moncton as cheaply as they can be built anywhere; the head offices are there; the railway men are there; it is a railway centre. Large numbers of our good men have been employed in the town of Amherst in the building of cars, and they are special artists in that line. I should be glad indeed if they were taken to the city of Moncton and allowed to pursue their vocation there, and to earn a living for themselves and for their families. I believe that this would be an advantage to the Intercolonial railway as well, and I hope that the matter will be taken seriously into consideration by the minister.

Country Harbour Is the centre of a long range of coast, it is the best port on the Atlantic coast or in Nova Scotia, and I would regard it as a great mistake if the minister did not include it in the original proposal. The sea can be reached at Country Harbour at a much
shorter distance from Sunnybrae than it can be at Guysborough.
Then you would rather have it go to Country Harbour than to Guysborough ?

Not at all; I do not care to accept anything less than the old proposal made originally by the late Government, which included a branch to Guysborough and also one to Country Harbour.
I do not think that anything else than that will be satisfactory, and I submit that if the minister will look into the possibilities of the traffic along that coast he will agree with me. I wish to say most emphatically that Country Harbour should be included in his proposal. That is all I have to say, and it is something I ought to say, because this is a matter of very great importance in my constituency. The disappointment will be very great in that part of the country when the minister's attitude is known.
Is Country Harbour developed in any way?

There are very slight
facilities. There is a public wharf and some shipping, but nothing further. We want the railway to develop it.
If the road were built without facilities it would not be of much use?
If it were reached by a railway there is no doubt in my mind that the trade would grow very rapidly.

I know that. I am
not joking about the matter; I am in earnest about it. The railway would not be of much use to Country Harbour until the harbour was developed ?

The railway, if built,
would involve a wharf at the end of it, where ships could load and unload, and that would be all the development that we would expect at the present time. That, I suppose, would be a part of the minister's proposals. The diversion at North Sydney and Sydney Mines improves the condition of the road there immensely and enables you, in the operation of the road, to get clear of two heavy grades. Is it in contemplation to better the grades at other points between Sydney and the straits?

There is a very heavy grade near River Denys.
There are a lot of them.

That is about the worst. The old saying is that the strength of the chain is equal to that if its weakest link. There is not much use of improving the grades around Sydney unless you are able to overcome these other grades. I think some surveys were made about the Grand Narrows and at River Denys. I would like to know if there is any immediate prospect of having these grades removed so as to provide the road with as nearly uniform grades as possible.

There has been a survey made and it seems to show that the improvement could be made at a less cost than by reducing the grades on the present road. Unfortunately, if we built another line we would have to run both the old and the new lines, because there is quite a settlement along the present line which would need the service, and we would have to give it. We have come to the conclusion, I think, that we will cut down some of the grades and renew the bridges so that we may be able to put on heavier rolling stock and heavier power for the present, anyway. To reduce the grades down to .06, with compensation, would cost about $58,000 a mile. It would cost in the neighbourhood of something like $45,000 a mile to go out by way of St. Peter's. The operation would cost just about double, as my hon. friend knows. The situation is such that we think the best plan now is to cut down the worst grades, increase the bridges and to put on heavier power.

I would like to ask the minister if he has considered the report of Engineer Clark, whom he sent down to Inverness county last summer, with regard to the projected line of railway in Inverness county?
I have not given very much attention to it.

I have just read over a part of the report, which the hon. minister handed to me a moment ago, which indicates that this proposed line will cost very much more than was estimated by the minister's representative Mr. Tessier who went down there three years ago. I am disappointed. to say the least. The report ends up by holding out very little encouragement for the construction of this piece of road. It will be sad and discouraging news

for the people of Inverness when they hear that the Government have practically abair-doned the idea of constructing this road.
I do not say that.

I think the report would indicate that very clearly. Perhaps I may be too pessimistic, but I have very good reason to be so. iSince I have had the honour of a seat in this House I have kept this matter before the Government-the late Government and the present one. I had hoped that when the facts of this proposition were properly submitted to the Government they would undertake the construction of this road from a business standpoint if for no other reason. I succeeded so well with the late Government that I got their assurance that they would undertake the construction of the line in the summer of 1912, not as a favour but as a practical business proposition. After the defeat of the Liberal Government the people of Inverness county sent a delegation to wait upon the Minister of Railways, and I had the honour of associating myself with these gentlemen when they met the minister, and they were received verv courteously by him. They laid the facts before him, not in as full detail as I would like, but they did as well as time permitted.
I suggested to the minister that he should send one of his own engineers there to look over the line. The hon. minister remembers this. The minister was kind enough to grant my request and he sent Mr. Tessier, who, I understand, is an engineer of very great experience in railway work. Mr. Tessier spent some time in the county of Inverness and gathered a very considerable number of facts, and the only fault I have to find with his report is that there were a great many items of possible traffic along that route which he failed to enumerate,_ the reason being that he did not stay long enough there to go into all the details. The reason I refer to his report at all is, that as to the cost of construction he was 'quite definite, and made an extended investigation and study of the whole route, and be assured the minister that the road would cost in the vicinity of $23,000 a mile only. I asked the minister last year his opinion about this report, and his reply was that in his judgment the report was too rosy. We heard nothing more about this until last summer, I saw a gentleman going through the county of Inverness. He called at the town of Inverness and took with him a gentleman, Mr. H. A. McEachen, barrister, there

and they drove to Cheticamp and came back the next day, and no doubt they enjoyed the very pleasant drive along the coast. As to how they could gather much information with respect to the road, I could never find out. They called at my own town, Margaree, on returning, and one would think that the Government would expect its officers to pay the representative of the people of that county the courtesy of calling on him to discuss the question with him, but that was not done.
I thought it possible this gentleman might call on me, but instead of that he called together a number of the political friends of the Minister of Railways and they discussed railway matters'!' Then these gentlemen went through the country and announced that this Mr. x Clark had assured them that the Government was going to undertake the construction of this road. Mr. Clark and Mr. McEachen went on to Orangedale and I heard nothing more about them. I find that this gentleman in his report to the minister enters into a long statement as to the probable cost of the construction of this road, and as I expect he added several thousand dollars more to the total cost of the line than at first estimated by Mr. Tessier. No doubt for the purpose of destroying the rosiness of this gentleman's report. That of course, in itself, if true, is calculated to justify the minister in not undertaking the construction of this road. This second engineer, Mr. Clark, who spent about a week there, was apparently able to furnish the minister with an itemized statement as to the cost of construction, which would indicate that the road would cost about $14,000 more than Mr. Tessier reported it would cost, although Mr. Tessier spent four months there gathering information upon which to base his report. It is a marvel to me how this second man could have gathered all this information on this joyride he had in the county of Inverness-because, to my mind, it was nothing more or less than a joyride.
You know what a joyride is, I do not.

I do not know very
much about it either, but I have heard something about it. I have spent some fifteen or twenty years in the practice oi my profession in a country district, and I have never felt very much joy in driving, but evidently this engineer did because he felt very comfortable driving along the country road in the cool of the evening in order no doubt to avoid heat of the midday
sun; of course he was a gentleman. _ It will be bad news to the people of Inverness if the minister does not now promise that this road will be built. From all the information in the possession of the minister, he must be convinced that this is a practical business proposition which there is ample merit to justify him undertaking, even if for no other purpose than to furnish additional earnings to the Intercolonial railway. I made the statement in this House two years ago that none of the lines discussed by hon. gentlemen here had half as much merit as this line in Inverness county. I have already enumerated the various sources of traffic, and I will not detain the House to repeat them now, but the minister has, without doubt, sufficient information in his possession, to cause him to see that this is a most meritorious piece of railway, so far as earning power is concerned. I can tell the minister that all the wealth of that rich county must remain dormant until this road is constructed. We have gold, iron, coal, copper, silver barytes and several other minerals, all of first-class quality and almost inexhaustable quantity; we have a first-class fishing industry which would in the fishing season furnish this road with regular and very considerable quantities of freight; and as fine a farming country as can be seen in any part of Canada, and a wealth of forest which as yet practically has not been touched; but all must remain hnexploited. until railway /transportation facilities are afforded. We can never expect to get our natural ressources developed in any other way than by railway construction, because along the coast of Inverness from Port Hood north, it is most difficult to create -adequate harbours for shipping. I hope the minister will revise his opinion that nothing can be done at present because that is a most indefinite assurance to these suffering people. We have had many surveys and many estimates as to the cost of this road, and the minister has even sent his accredited representative there, to furnish him with a report, and an honest report it is, I have no doubt. There is another report from the engineer who went down last year on this famous trip I have referred to, which is based on information gathered in a few- days, which I noted clapped on $14,000 a mile in addition to the estimate of the former engineer's estimate, and now it is time to get down to businef -. I trust that the Minister of Railways will change his mind and go on with this work.

and thus confer a lasting benefit on my constituency and on the Government railway' system. Last year, I had faith in the hon. minister. I have not lost that faith altogether, it has been almost wrecked by the language of this report of Mr. Clark's and of the minister who will not say that the road will be built.

I expect so. But I hope the trade will increase first. I was talking it over with the manager last week, and he thought about the 1st or 2nd of May he might start it again.

When this railway was operated by the company, a small station was used about a quarter of a mile from the main Sackville station. train is directly across the street. To correct this would be only a matter of moving this small station-which is very small, not more than 20 by 30 feet-a short distance, so that when the train stops the engine or cars will not be across the street.

Next year the expenses of these lines will go in with the working expenses of the whole system. We would like to keep the expenses separate at first just to see how it works out. That may not be an easy task, either.

I think the minister is right in endeavouring to do this, either for his own information or for the benefit of the public, but on account of the through freight it will not be an easy thing to do. The rates now paid on these lines are absolutely local.

We have kept them
so.

When it comes to be part of the Intercolonial the rates will have to be merged into a thorough rate, and evidently these branch lines, if traffic does not increase, will not be as remunerative as they are now. present. On the other hand, the people shipping goods will get the benefit of lower -rates. I suppose the minister is not in a position to tell how the International or New Brunswick has paid.

The International pays working expenses, and we have not yet ^changed the rates. After this legislation passes we will have to give through rates and therefore lower rates. Quebec bridge, construction, $3,500,000.

Could the minister tell
us how this is getting on, when it is likely

to be completed and how the company that got the contract is doing?

The stonework is
completed and a splendid job it is. It cost a little less than the estimate. I have a sketch here that shows the work if my hon. friend will look at it.

How much will it cost
altogether?

Including the old
bridge the estimate is between $30,000,000 and $35,000,000.

Leaving out the old
bridge, how much will the carrying out of the contract for this bridge cost?

$17,000,000 for the
new bridge. The contract for the steel is at the rate of so mucn per pound.
We made a contract for the superstructure outside of the piers altogether. Will the superstructure cost $17,000,000?

That includes the
piers.

Has the minister heard
any complaint lately from the British firm that did not get the contract?

Welland ship canal construction, $5,500,000.

Would the minister
state if any progress is being made towards the construction of the water main which it is proposed to lay from Lake Erie in order to supply Welland, St. Catharines, Thorold and Merritton which have been taking water from the canal?

It has not been
started yet but I hope to be able to get it started this summer. I discussed it with the chief engineer of the canal and he thinks we had better do it by day work. It is important to get it done properly because it is a thing that must stand forever and he thinks that better than letting a contract. We have not decided whether we will do it by day labour or by contract, but I hope it will be started this summer in order to give these places water before turning the river in.

I am not interested in whether it is done by day labour or contract, because if it is done under Mr. MARCH 29, 1915
Weller's supervision it will be done properly and economically. The question is: will it be done?
It is provided for in these estimates.
And the work will likely be commenced this summer.
I hope so.
Has it been absolutely decided to put the river and the canal on the same level?
We will have to turn the river in.
I was not sure it had been absolutely decided to do that.
That is his scheme.
How many contracts have been let?
Five. .
How many are there to be let and when does the minister expect the work to be completed.

There are four contracts to let. No. 3 contract is the heaviest of all, and even starting this year I think we could complete these five by the time contract No. 3 is finished, which will, we hope, be three years from now, but I am afraid we may be a little shy on that. '
What is the size of the lock?
800 feet long, 85 feet wide, and 30 feet deep on the sills. The dredging will only go to 25 feet but they can keep on dredging year after year.

There is a cut off at Humberstone, where a kind of guardlock is to be constructed. That section will take more than three years and could not the minister find it justifiable to let the contract this year and begin work on that section.
That will have to be discussed with Mr. Weller and my colleagues.
They want to go on if the minister can find the money.

That is a point I have to discuss with my colleagues.
Towards construction of railway to connect Montreal with National Transcontinental railway, $750,000.
Will the minister explain this?

In 1912 we gave a subsidy to the North Railway Company, and last session they came back again and wanted a guarantee, and a guarantee was promised to them; but before they got to work they wanted a guarantee and a subsidy both, and the Government concluded in that case they had better build the road themselves. The hon. member for Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) and others expressed the opinion that these people ought to be compensated for the surveys they had made and other expenditures they had gone to. They got a charter and a land grant from Quebec of 8,000 acres a mile up to where it touched the Transcontinental, and 10,000 a mile beyond that, and then they had a subsidy from this Parliament. They have given up all their rights, and this was the amount that was allowed them on their handing their surveys and everything they had over to the Government. Their claim was $900,000, but we would not entertain that.
Is the Government going to use these surveys?
As far as we can; I think we will use a great portion of them.
Where does the road run from Montreal?
It runs through the county of Argenteuil; it has to conform with the physical conditions of thg country.
Are there estimates as to the cost of the road?
No. They said it would be an expensive road and would cost $50,000 or $60,000 a mile.
What standard road will be built?

If the Government built it it must be the standard of the Transcontinental railway, because it is intended to give Montreal direct connection with the Transcontinental railway, and it would be foolish to build any other kind of a road.
Are you going on witli the road this year?
I do not think so.-
The minister is not sure he will go on with it this year, and he probably will not.

I insisted on having
' the vote in because conditions may change and no one knows when the war may end.
Are you not likely to be accused, as you have accused others, of starting to build a road before you know what it will cost?
We will not do that.
You have spent a quarter of a million dollars on it already.
Yes, but that was for surveys and there were various other expenditures which the company had gone to. It was not all for building a railway.
They will not build any railway.
That is true.
I think in the first place there was a subsidy offered to any company that would build the road, and then it was transferred to a particular company, and this is the particular company.

That is right.
Soulanges canal, protection works, $24,500.

I suppose, as a matter
of fact, the expenditures for repairs on these canals will have to be continued so long as you have canals.
Yes, we cannot help it.
As long as the work is needed and the money is judiciously expended there cannot he any question about it. This work has been discussed on several occasions and it has been going on for a long. time.

I think you let the
contract.
Trent canal construction, $1,500,000 ; to pay claim of Cory and Laverdure, $16,000.
When will this work be completed?
They expect that the Rice Lake division will be completed in October, 1916. There is one contract not yet let.
Does the minister expect that the contract for remaining section on the Severn river will be let this year?
No.

Has the question about
the water powers on the Trent canal been settled amicably, or is it still in court?
I think we will have to wait for the Privy Council- to decide that:
Is the case before the Privy Council?

They have put in their statement of claim, but I do not think it has gone to trial yet. The Justice Department has had more than it could do since the war commenced, and the case has not been prepared for trial.
As I remember it, Cory and Laverdure put in their claim for work done years ago, and these several claims were submitted to the chief engineer, Mr. Schreiber.
No, they were submitted to Joseph Hobson, Robert Surtees, and George P. Brophy.

That was the commission they were referred to, but Mr. Schreiber was the engineer. The claims, except this particular one, went through with the approval of every person.
There are minute details about it that I cannot recall to mind, but I remember that Mr. Cory discussed it with me several times, and I thought he had no claim, after I had read the documents many times and had consulted Mr. Schreiber. Some statement that he had made to Mr. Schreiber, if I remember well, put him out of court on this item. With the information before me, I declined to pay him. Perhaps the minister has some new information.

I took my facts largely from the report and findings of this commission of engineers. It seemed to me that from an equitable standpoint he wasr entitled to this amount of money. He asked for a great deal more-$30,000 or $35,000. After going through it many times and discussing it, it seemed to me that he was equitably entitled to this money. He does not get over fifty per cent of his claim.
'Mr. GRAHAM: I am the last man to find fault with the settlement of a claim on equitable grounds as against legal technicalities.
Legally he was out of court.

There are many claims- I suppose there are still-that have some foundation in equity, though not in law, and I would not object to their all being cleaned up in an equitable manner. I think the Government has no more right to

beat a man on technical grounds than one man would have a right to refuse to pay an account to another on technical grounds if he really owed the money. If the minister has come to the conclusion that the country owes Cory & Laverdure $16,000, I have no objection. All I am saying is that I looked into the matter, and I thought, with the facts before me, that they were not entitled to the money.

As the hon. gentleman says, there are many of these claims. Mr. Cleveland has been here to get me to go into his claim. I have not done it yet. The claim is very old; the engineers on the ground at the time are gone. It is hard to work out what is due him in equity. I could not do it this year, but I believe there is something due him, and I hope to get at it,
What is the reason against him?
He is outlawed for one thing.
That does not matter.
The claim was more for extras, outside the contract itself. It was in the department even before my hon. friend (Mr. Graham) was minister.
Long before.

It was a difference between Mr. Schreiber and the Board of Engineers.

Canals - compassionate allowance to the widow of the late Michael Lawrence Allen, who was accidentally killed while in discharge of his duties as handy-man on the Lachine canal, $1,000. *

I am glad that the minister has put in items 362 and 363, compassionate allowances, and I want him to add one more. I brought to the attention of the minister the other night the matter of paying compensation to Mr. O'Rourke, who lost his wife under conditions similar to those in respect of these other two votes.

My hon. friend says
that he would obtain further information and speak to me about it, but I have not received that information.

I will give it to my hon.
friend now. The hon. gentleman has information in his office with regard to this man's wife having been killed. Application was made for compensation. I was glad to hear my hon. friend say that he allowed these other claims to pass not on legal grounds, but on equitable grounds. I think he took the right ground.
Cases are not at all similar.

But the precedent is similar and my hon. friend's argument is similar. While perhaps this man legally was out of court, equitably he was entitled to some consideration. I have received information that this man is in a very delicate state of health; he is partially paralysed and has hard work to get along. When a compassionate allowance is made in these two cases one might also be made in his case. I know it would be gratefully received by him and would be appreciated by the people generally.

The Supplementary
Estimates for 1915-16 will be down in the morning, so I am afraid it would be too late to get anything in this year, even if my hon. friend's new information would convince me that an allowance should be made.
